levels.title: Aid groups scramble to help as Israel-Hamas war intensifies
levels.body:
Aid groups are scrambling to help people caught in the war between Israel and Hamas. Israel is a country in the Middle East. Hamas is an armed Palestinian group. Palestine is a state in the Middle East. Israel and Hamas are fighting in and around Gaza by the Mediterranean Sea. Gaza is home to 2.3 million people. It is Palestine's largest city. The aid groups have to decide on how to get help to people safely.

Hamas fighters took the world by surprise on October 7, 2023. They made surprise attacks against Israel. Israel fought back. The country's soldiers sent planes to strike targets in Gaza. Israel also stopped food and other supplies from going into Gaza.

Hundreds Killed and Wounded On Both Sides

The United Nations (U.N.) and aid groups are worried about working in the area. Hundreds of people have been killed. Thousands have been wounded on both sides. Aid groups say there are needs both in Gaza and Israel. They are begging to be allowed into Gaza to help Palestinians stuck in the middle of the fighting.

The Egyptian Red Crescent is one aid group. It sent more than 2 tons (2,000 pounds) of supplies to Gaza. Efforts to organize food and other deliveries are underway. The U.N. and other aid agencies were talking with Egypt about how to send aid to Gaza. The area is surrounded by armed forces. The groups were looking at a crossing point between the strip and the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt.

Meanwhile, the World Health Organization said its supplies have already been used up in seven hospitals in Gaza. It was working on getting funds. It would buy more supplies from local markets.

Sharing Medical Supplies

Doctors Without Borders is still working in Gaza. The aid group has to depend on medical supplies it already has in Gaza. It can't bring any more supplies in.

Doctors Without Borders says it runs programs in Palestine because Israel has strong emergency and health services. The group is helping patients in Gaza and giving supplies to other hospitals. The hospitals have become overcrowded with patients. They are running out of medicine.

Doctors Without Borders said it may run out of supplies. These supplies are used to operate on wounded patients.

EU Weighs In On Conflict

Governments have also been weighing how to respond. The European Union (EU) is a 27-nation group. On October 9 it said it might stop aid for Palestine in the wake of Hamas' attacks on Israel. Germany and Austria are two countries in Europe. They also said they were stopping aid for Palestine.

Meanwhile, some groups are stepping up aid work in Israel. Many people have left their homes because of the war.

Hadassah, The Women's Zionist Organization of America, is an aid group. It said its center is treating wounded Israeli soldiers and other people. About 90 percent of the patients in the center are soldiers. The center also accepts anyone who's wounded or injured.

Palestine Children's Relief Fund helps children who need to travel to the U.S. for medical care. Because of the war, the group will help in other ways. It will provide food, medication, clothing and other types of aid.

They are typically the first to be brought in for traumatic injuries. The center also accepts anyone who's wounded or injured.

It runs programs to support people with disabilities, the elderly and children and families who've been affected by the war and prior conflicts. It was working with its partners to address the emergency. Its partners include the Israeli government.

levels.title: Aid groups scramble to help as Israel-Hamas war intensifies
levels.body:
On October 10, 2023, aid groups were scrambling to assist people caught in the war between Israel and Hamas. They are determining what aid operations are safe to continue. Efforts are being complicated by an intensified Israeli blockade of Gaza and continued fighting.

Hamas fighters went on an attack that took the world by surprise on October 7. They attacked Israel without warning. They killed and wounded many Israeli people and took some captive. Israel responded by ordering airstrikes on Gaza. It also cut off food, fuel and other supplies from going into the territory. The United Nations (U.N.) and aid groups operating in the area became concerned about these moves. Gaza is home to 2.3 million people. Hamas, in turn, pledged to kill Israelis it took captive if the country's military bombs targeted people in Gaza without warning.

Hundreds Killed On Both Sides Of Conflict

Hundreds of people have been killed and thousands wounded on both sides. Aid groups operating in the region say there are needs both in Gaza and Israel. More than 2 tons (2,000 pounds) of medical supplies from the Egyptian Red Crescent have been sent to Gaza. Similar to the Red Cross, the Red Crescent is a humanitarian aid society. Efforts are underway to organize food and other deliveries, said an Egyptian military official. But the United Nations and other aid groups are pleading for more access to Palestinians who find themselves in the middle of intense fighting.

The U.N. and other aid agencies were working with Egypt to send aid to the besieged Gaza, said an Egyptian official and aid worker on October 10. It would be through a crossing point between the strip and Egypt's Sinai Peninsula. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization said its medical supplies in seven hospitals in Gaza had already been used up. It was shifting funds to purchase more from local markets.

Doctors Without Borders is still operating in Gaza. It has to rely on supplies it already has inside the territory because it can't bring more in, said Emmanuel Massart. He's a deputy desk coordinator with the organization.

The group says it only runs programs in Palestinian areas because Israel has strong emergency and health services. It reported on October 9 that it provided treatments to more than 50 people following airstrikes north of Gaza City. The group said it is helping patients in Gaza and donating medical supplies to other clinics and hospitals. The centers have become overcrowded with patients. There are also shortages of drugs and fuel that can be used for generators.

If Doctors Without Borders is not able to resupply quickly, Massart said, it will run out of supplies to operate on wounded patients. He also said the organization's centers are running on generators due to the low supply of electricity. Cutting off fuel will present a "huge problem," he said.

"Looks Like It's Going To Get Worse"

Mercy Corps' work has also been disturbed by the war. It has been providing people in Gaza with food and water. Right now, the group said the team on the ground is trying to find a scenario that would enable them to get back to work. The blockade of food and other supplies into Gaza is a major worry.

"We are very concerned with the way things are going at this point because it looks like it's going to get worse — very soon," said Arnaud Quemin. He's the Middle East regional director for the organization. The sealing of Gaza, he said, will increase the need for aid "very quickly."

Governments have also been weighing how to respond. As the fighting intensified, the European Union (EU), a 27-nation group, announced on October 9 that it would review the assistance it provides in the wake of Hamas' attacks on Israel. Germany and Austria said they were suspending development aid for Palestinian areas.

Helping Those In Need

Meanwhile, some organizations are stepping up aid efforts in Israel.

Hadassah, The Women's Zionist Organization of America, said its center in Jerusalem is treating wounded Israeli soldiers and citizens. About 90 percent of the patients in the center are soldiers. They are typically the first to be brought in for traumatic injuries. The center also accepts anyone who is wounded or injured.

The American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee said on October 8 that it was activating its emergency response team in Israel. It runs programs to support people with disabilities, the elderly and children and families who've been affected by the war and prior conflicts. The organization said it was working with its partners, including the Israeli government, to address what it called an emergency never seen before.

One organization that helps Palestinian children is shifting its focus, too. Palestine Children's Relief Fund is a U.S.-based charity that helps children in need travel to the U.S. for medical treatment. Given the war, the fund is shifting from long-term programs toward more urgent needs for food, medication, clothing and other types of aid. The group noted the blockade and security risks to its Gaza staff make it more challenging to do that.

"There are no areas of security, there are no safe havens," said Steve Sosebee, the president of Palestine Children's Relief Fund. "And therefore, it's very difficult for us to be out in the field."

"If you're a teacher now, if you know the children are traumatized, you need special skills and special training in order to manage what you're experiencing and provide for the emotional needs, which are extraordinary at this time, of your youngest charges," Zwang said.

He noted the blockade and security risks to its Gaza staff make it more challenging to do that.

"There are no areas of security, there are no safe havens," Sosebee said. "And therefore, it's very difficult for us to be out in the field … when there are no safe places from the constant bombing and attacks that are taking place over the last 72 hours."

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: Aid groups scramble to help as Israel-Hamas war intensifies
levels.body:
NEW YORK, New York — Humanitarian groups on October 10, 2023, were scrambling to assist civilians caught in the war between Israel and Hamas and determine what aid operations were still safe to continue — efforts that were being complicated by an intensified Israeli blockade of Gaza and continued fighting.

Two days after Hamas militants went on an attack that took the world by surprise, Israel increased airstrikes on Gaza and blocked off food, fuel and other supplies from going into the territory, a move that raised concerns at the United Nations and among aid groups operating in the area that is home to 2.3 million people. Hamas, in turn, pledged to kill Israelis it abducted if the country's military bombs civilian targets in Gaza without warning.

Hundreds of people have been killed and thousands wounded on both sides, and aid groups operating in the region say there are needs both in Gaza and Israel.

More than 2 tons of medical supplies from the Egyptian Red Crescent have been sent to Gaza and efforts are underway to organize food and other deliveries, according to an Egyptian military official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to talk to the press. But the United Nations (U.N.) and other aid groups are pleading for more access to help Palestinians who find themselves in the middle of intense fighting.

The U.N. and other aid agencies were talking with Egypt to send humanitarian aid to the besieged Gaza through a crossing point between the strip and Egypt's Sinai Peninsula, an Egyptian official and aid worker said October 10. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization said medical supplies it has in seven hospitals in Gaza had already been used up and it was reprogramming funds to purchase more from local markets.

Doctors Without Borders, which is still operating in Gaza, has to rely on supplies it already has inside the territory because it can't bring any more in, said Emmanuel Massart, a deputy desk coordinator with the organization in Brussels.

The group — which says it only runs programs in Palestinian areas since Israel has strong emergency and health services — reported October 9 that it provided treatments to more than 50 people following airstrikes at the Jabalia refugee camp located north of Gaza City. In addition to helping patients in Gaza, it said it was donating medical supplies to other clinics and hospitals, which have become overcrowded with patients and are experiencing shortages of drugs, as well as fuel that can be used for generators.

If Doctors Without Borders is not able to resupply quickly, Massart said, it will run out of supplies it can use to operate on patients who might be wounded. He also said since the facilities the organization uses are running on generators due to the low supply of electricity, cutting off fuel will present a "huge problem."

"If there is no fuel anymore, there are no medical facilities anymore because we cannot run our medical facility without the energy," Massart said.

The war has also been deeply disruptive to work Mercy Corps has been doing to provide people in Gaza with necessities like food and water, said Arnaud Quemin, the Middle East regional director for the organization. Right now, he said the team on the ground is trying to find a scenario that would enable them to get back to work. The blockade of food and other supplies into Gaza is a major worry.

"We are very concerned with the way things are going at this point because it looks like it's going to get worse — very soon," Quemin said. The sealing of Gaza, he said, will create "humanitarian needs very quickly."

Governments have also been weighing how to respond.

As the fighting intensified, the European Union (EU) late October 9 reversed an earlier announcement by an EU commissioner that the bloc was "immediately" suspending aid for Palestinian authorities. Instead, the 27-nation group said it would urgently review the assistance it provides in the wake of Hamas' attacks on Israel. Two European countries — Germany and Austria — said they were suspending development aid for Palestinian areas.

Meanwhile, some organizations are stepping up aid efforts in Israel, which has seen displacement because of the violence.

Naomi Adler, CEO of Hadassah, The Women's Zionist Organization of America, said a trauma center in Jerusalem that's owned by the organization is treating wounded Israeli soldiers and civilians. About 90 percent of the patients in the center right now are soldiers, who are typically the first to be brought in for traumatic injuries, Adler said. But the center also accepts anyone who is wounded or injured in the country.

The American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee (JDC), a Jewish humanitarian organization, said on October 8 that it was activating its emergency response team in Israel, where it runs programs to support people with disabilities, the elderly and children and families who've been affected by the war and prior conflicts. The organization said it was working with its partners, including the Israeli government, to address what it called an unprecedented emergency.

JDC's CEO Ariel Zwang said that among other things, the nonprofit is helping teachers, social workers and other caregivers provide support to those who've suffered trauma and tragedies from the events of the past few days. She said it will help nursery teachers, for example, explain to children why some of their classmates are suddenly missing.

"If you're a teacher now, if you know the children are traumatized, you need special skills and special training in order to manage what you're experiencing and provide for the emotional needs, which are extraordinary at this time, of your youngest charges," Zwang said.

One organization that helps Palestinian children is shifting its focus, too. Steve Sosebee, the president of Palestine Children's Relief Fund, a U.S.-based charity that helps children in need travel to the U.S. for medical treatment, said given the war, the fund is now looking away from long-term programs and toward more urgent needs for food, medication, clothing and other types of basic humanitarian aid. But like others, he noted the blockade and security risks to its Gaza staff makes it more challenging to do that.

"There are no areas of security, there are no safe havens," Sosebee said. "And therefore, it's very difficult for us to be out in the field providing humanitarian aid when there are no safe places from the constant bombing and attacks that are taking place over the last 72 hours."

title: Asian Games offer a few sports you may not recognize, like kabaddi and wushu
zhTitle: 亚运会上你可能没见过的项目
reason: 卡巴迪、藤球、武术、库拉什，四套规则各自的说明。

cover.caption: China's Feng He (left) fights Iran's Mohsen Mohammadseifi in the Wushu men's 70 kilograms (154 pounds) final at the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, on September 28, 2023.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Asian Games offer a few sports you may not recognize, like kabaddi and wushu
levels.body:
The Asian Games started on September 23, 2023. They are being held in Hangzhou, China.

About 12,500 athletes participate in the games. That's more than the number of participants in the Olympic games. The Asian Games highlight sports that are more popular in Asia. Read on to learn more about them.

Kabaddi

Kabaddi is pronounced kuh-bud-DEE. It started in India and is very popular there. It draws millions of viewers. The sport does not use clubs or rackets. There are no goals. There is not even a ball.

Here's how it is played. Two teams have seven players each. They play on a small court. A single player on the offense is called a "raider." The raider crosses the centerline and tries to touch as many players as possible on the other side. They only have 30 seconds to do so. Then, they have to return across the centerline without being tackled. The game is played in two 20-minute periods. Points are earned by tagging opponents or by stopping the raider.

Sepaktakraw

Sepaktakraw started in Malaysia. The sport is like volleyball. But players can't use their hands. Players are on each side of a 5-foot-high net. The ball is kicked back and forth over the net. The goal is to get the ball to hit the ground on the opponent's side of the net. The sport has also been known as "kick volleyball" in the United States. The ball is smaller than a volleyball, though. It's closer to the size of a large melon.

Wushu

Wushu has been part of the Asian Games since 1990. It is the Chinese term for "martial arts." Wushu competition takes place in two distinct areas.

One area of competition is performing routines. Athletes show off different ways to attack and defend. The other area of Wushu competition is the full-contact version of the sport. It is often called Chinese kickboxing.

China won 10 gold medals in wushu at the 2018 Asian Games. Iran, Indonesia and Macau also won medals in the sport. Macau is part of China. China won gold medals in both the men's and women's finals this year.

Kurash

Kurash is a form of wrestling. It started in Central Asia. The sport is thousands of years old. It was first introduced into the Asian Games five years ago. At the time, Uzbekistan won a gold medal in the sport. Iran, Mongolia, Taiwan and India also won multiple medals in 2018.

figures.caption: China's Feng He (left) fights Iran's Mohsen Mohammadseifi in the Wushu men's 70 kilograms (154 pounds) final at the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, on September 28, 2023.
India's Sonali Vishnu Shingate (in blue) is caught by Iran team members during the women's team kabaddi gold medal match at the 18th Asian Games in Jakarta, Indonesia, on August 24, 2018.
Japan's Toshitaka Naito (center) kicks a ball against Indonesia's team during the men's quadrant gold medal match at the 18th Asian Games in Palembang, Indonesia, on September 1, 2018.
Iran's Hanieh Rajabi competes in the Wushu Women's Nanquan competition at the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, on September 26, 2023.
Indonesia's Terry Kusumawardani Susanti (right) competes against Vietnam's Nguyen Ngoc Ngan during a women's kurash match at the 18th Asian Games in Jakarta, Indonesia, on August 28, 2018.

levels.name: 基础
levels.title: Asian Games offer a few sports you may not recognize, like kabaddi and wushu
levels.body:
Sports like basketball and volleyball are fun to watch. But if you are tired of those and are looking for something new to watch, why not check out some of the sports in the Asian Games? The event kicked off on September 23, 2023, in Hangzhou, China.

The Asian Games have many Olympic events such as archery, boxing and water polo. Some events offer qualifying spots for next year's Paris Olympics. However, the main focus of the games is on sports that are popular in Asia. About 12,500 athletes participate in the games. That's more than the number of participants in the Olympic games. They represent 45 nations and territories.

Some of the popular sports include kabaddi, sepaktakraw, wushu and kurash. The Asian Games also feature "mind sports" such as bridge, chess, xiangqi (known as Chinese chess) and others.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Barbie "chooses" Women in Sports for Career of the Year
levels.body:
This year, Mattel's Barbie put the spotlight on Women in Sports. The company chose this for its Career of the Year.

Jen Welter was blown away.

"As a little girl, I didn't have this," she said. Welter was the first female coach in the National Football League. The Arizona Cardinals hired her in 2015.

Welter never imagined herself coaching football. "There was no one who looked like me," she said.

Some jobs hire more men than women. But that does not have to be true in the future. Mattel is the company that makes Barbie. It hopes the dolls in this collection will help girls to dream big.

This year's collection highlights four sports careers: general manager, coach, referee and sports reporter.

The First Female General Manager In Baseball

A report came out in 2021. It looked at the number of women in sports writing careers. Only a small number worked in sports writing.

Even fewer women are sports team managers. In 2020, Kim Ng was hired by the Miami Marlins. They are a baseball team. Ng was the first female general manager in Major League Baseball. There still aren't any in football, basketball or hockey.

"Every first was impossible until it wasn't," Welter said. Her dad helped her become confident. He taught her to fish. He trusted her to reel in the biggest fish.

Later, Welter started playing football. She became a running back on a professional men's team. She was the first woman to do that, too.

A Role Model For Women Coaches

Wendell Davis encouraged her to become a coach. Davis played for the Dallas Cowboys. "I [without thinking] said, 'No, girls don't coach football,'" Welter said.

But Davis knew what to do. He told the team that Welter would coach.

Welter became a great role model. More women have become coaches because of her. There were 15 female coaches in the NFL in 2022. There were also three female referees last season.

Welter said that dreaming is the first step. "Once you have that dream, you can do the work. You're driven to do the same things that the guys are doing."

figures.caption: Over the years, Barbie has featured dolls of various careers, from doctor to firefighter to veterinarian. The theme for Career of the Year 2023 is "Women in Sports," featuring a general manager, coach, referee and sports reporter (not pictured above).

Jen Welter, a former defensive specialist coach for the Atlanta Legends, walks the field before a game at the Georgia State stadium in 2019. She reflects on her career in football after finding out about Barbie's 2023 Career of the Year doll line.
Kim Ng also breaks boundaries as the first female general manager in MLB. She holds the position of general manager of the Miami Marlins.

levels.body:
"As a little girl, I didn't have this," Jen Welter said. She was blown away after finding out Mattel's Barbie had chosen Women in Sports for her Career of the Year.

Welter was the first female coach in the National Football League (NFL). The Arizona Cardinals hired her in 2015. She said that she didn't imagine herself coaching football.

"There was no one who looked like me," said Welter. She was also the first woman to play running back on a professional men's team. "Football was the first place in the world that somebody told me that girls and boys did different things."

The Barbie collection highlights four sports careers: general manager, coach, referee and sports reporter. Mattel hopes to encourage girls to get involved in sports.

Mattel has highlighted more than 250 careers with Barbie. The company wants to inspire girls to get jobs in fields where women often don't work.

The First Female General Manager In Baseball

In 2021, Associated Press Sports Editors released a report on women in sports careers. It showed how few women there are in sports journalism. A little over 16 percent of sports editors, reporters and column writers are women.

In 2020, the Miami Marlins hired Kim Ng. That made her the first female general manager in Major League Baseball. However, there are currently no female general managers in football, basketball or hockey. Women have been hired in assistant manager roles, though.

"Every first was impossible until it wasn't," Welter said. She said that her dad helped her gain confidence as a child. She credited him for her belief that things should be decided on ability, not tradition.

"He let me go fishing with the boys. It wasn't like he only let me take the rod when it was a small fish. He believed if it was your fish, you took it, and you either caught it, or you didn't. When I finally got an opportunity to try out for my first football team, it was the same thing."

"After I played in pro football, he told me I had to coach," Welter said. She was referring to former Dallas Cowboy Wendell Davis. "I [without thinking] said, 'No, girls don't coach football.' Thankfully, he took the job on my behalf and told me about it later."

Paving A Path For Future Women

Davis told Welter that her choice was bigger than she was. If she quit, "the entire [story] surrounding women coaching in men's pro football would be about how there once had been a woman, but she quit."

She didn't quit. Instead, Welter paved a path for future women on the sidelines. By the 2022 season, there were 15 female coaches in the NFL. There were three female game officials last season. The college all-star game the Hula Bowl even had an all-female officiating crew in 2023.

Welter said that her presence on the sidelines provides a visible example of what girls can become. "Girls could say, 'That looks cool. I want to do that.' Now you have a brand like Barbie, with a big giant corporation like Mattel, saying they want to change this for girls. This is how we're going to start. That doesn't mean it's a finish. It's a start."

She said that the permission to dream is the first step toward imagining what you can become. "Once you have that dream, you can do the work. You're driven to do the same things that the guys are doing. But if we don't have that early idea, then where does that same permission come from?"

Barbie commits to empowering the next generation of female leaders in sports. To do so, Barbie is partnering with VOICEINSPORT. This group connects and inspires girls through sports.

Thankfully, he took the job on my behalf and told me about it later. He said I couldn't quit, or the entire story surrounding women coaching in men's pro football would be about how there once had been a woman, but she quit."

She didn't quit, instead paving a path for future women on the sidelines. By the 2022 season, there were 15 female coaches in the NFL, and there were also three female game officials last season. The college all-star game the Hula Bowl even had an all-female officiating crew in 2023.

Welter said that her presence on the sidelines provides a visible example of what girls can accomplish and become. "Girls could say, 'That looks cool. I want to do that.' Now you have a brand like Barbie, with a big giant corporation like Mattel, saying they want to change this for girls. This is how we're going to start. That doesn't mean it's a finish. It's a start."

In addition to the new collection, Barbie is committed to supporting and empowering the next generation of female leaders in sports. To do so, Barbie has partnered with VOICEINSPORT, a community that connects and inspires girls through sports.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Biden uses executive power to create a New Deal-style American Climate Corps
levels.body:
The United States government is trying to fight climate change. This is the significant change in the climate of Earth. It happens over a long period of time. Climate change can happen naturally. Today, human activities largely cause climate change.

The U.S created a major program. The program is called the American Climate Corps.

This climate corps will create jobs for more than 20,000 people. They will all work on protecting the environment. President Joe Biden approved this program.

First Tried As A Law

Many people have wanted a climate corps for years. These people include activists and some lawmakers. They have been asking Biden to make it possible.

Some lawmakers wrote him a letter. In it, they wrote about storms, heat waves and fires in this past year. They said that the government needed to do something big.

Then Biden approved the creation of the climate corps. It is modeled after a program from the 1930s. That was called the Civilian Conservation Corps. President Franklin D. Roosevelt created it. That program created many jobs, too. It helped the country during the Great Depression.

Many Jobs With One Purpose

Many people are happy about the climate corps. Not everyone thinks it is a good idea, though. Some lawmakers think the climate corps is a waste of money.

The White House did not say how much the program will cost. It also did not say how it will be paid for.

Workers in the climate corps will do all kinds of jobs. Some will help protect coasts from storms and high water. Some will plant trees. Others will work on sun and wind power. They will do many other jobs, too.

Everyone will have one thing in common, though. They will be working on protecting the environment and the people who live in it.

levels.name: 基础
levels.title: Biden uses executive power to create a New Deal-style American Climate Corps
levels.body:
The United States government is about to create a major program to fight climate change. It is called the American Climate Corps. Climate change is the significant change in the climate of Earth over a long period of time. It can happen naturally, but today, climate change is largely caused by human activities.

President Joe Biden approved this program in September 2023. It will train a huge work force to do jobs related to conservation, or protecting the environment.

The White House says the program will create jobs for more than 20,000 people. For example, some of these people will build trails and plant trees. Others will help install solar panels, devices that change energy from the sun into electricity.

First Tried As A Law

U.S. lawmakers had considered creating a climate corps before. However, lawmakers could not agree on it. Members of the Democratic Party wanted the plan to succeed, but members of the Republican Party strongly opposed it. They were concerned about the cost. As a result, the idea never went forward.

Democrats and environmental groups never gave up, though. They pushed Biden to issue an executive order allowing the creation of the climate corps. An executive order is a rule that the president can issue without the approval of Congress.

The Sunrise Movement is an environmental group that led the push for a climate corps. Its leader, Varshini Prakash, celebrated the announcement.

She said, "The path toward a Green New Deal is beginning to become visible." The Green New Deal is a plan for taking on climate change and creating new jobs. Many activists support the Green New Deal, but Republicans ridicule it. They say it would raise taxes and cost too much money.

"Young People Nationwide Are Excited"

On September 9, Prakash joined a White House call in support of the new job corps.

Prakash and other climate activists have not always supported Biden. They were furious after he approved a huge new oil-drilling project this spring. For now, though, they put those concerns aside as they hailed the new jobs program.

The climate corps is modeled after a 1930s program called the Civilian Conservation Corps. It was part of President Franklin D. Roosevelt's famous program called the New Deal. It created many jobs and helped the country through a hard period.

"Young people nationwide are excited to see the launch of the American Climate Corps,″ said Cristina Tzintzún Ramirez. Tzintzún Ramirez an activist, too. She says that young people care a lot about connecting climate issues with social issues. This is called climate justice. She added that now these people have the opportunity to fight for climate justice through their jobs.

A Strong Government Response To Climate Change

More than 50 Democratic lawmakers had also encouraged Biden to create a climate corps. They wrote a letter calling for a strong government response to climate change.

The lawmakers mentioned recent examples of climate-related disasters. They highlighted deadly heat waves, floods and wildfires.

Democrats called the creation of the climate corps "historic."

Many Jobs With One Purpose

The White House did not say how much the program will cost or how it will be paid for. Democrats said some money will come from laws passed in 2021 and 2022. They plan to use that money to create of thousands of jobs.

Republicans have largely dismissed the climate corps as a waste of money.

The climate corps will provide opportunities to work on many different projects. For example, some projects are aimed at protecting places called wetlands. These are wet, low-lying areas. This will help keep communities in those areas safe from storms and flooding. Other projects will focus on using natural sources, like the sun and wind, to power our lives. Meanwhile, other people will work on managing forests to prevent wildfires.

The climate corps is not the only big project meant to help the environment. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is also planning to give out a lot of money soon. The money will go to states and communities with plans to cut down their pollution.

The EPA's goal is to make the environment healthier in the future. They want to help communities create that future.

At the United Nations in New York, President Joe Biden met with government officials to discuss plans for the environment on September 19, 2023.

levels.body:
In September 2023, President Joe Biden approved the creation of a major program to fight climate change. It is called the American Climate Corps. It will train a huge work force to do jobs related to conservation, or protecting the environment.

First Tried As A Law

The climate corps had been proposed in early versions of the sweeping climate law approved in 2022. However, Republicans strongly opposed it, citing concerns about cost. As a result, the proposal was removed from the law.

Democrats and environmental activist groups never gave up on the plan, though. They pushed Biden to issue an executive order allowing the creation of the climate corps. An executive order is a rule that the president can issue without the approval of Congress.

The Sunrise Movement is an environmental group that led the push for a climate corps. Its executive director, Varshini Prakash, celebrated the announcement.

She said, "The path toward a Green New Deal is beginning to become visible." The Green New Deal is a plan for both taking on climate change and creating new jobs. Many activists support the program, but it is ridiculed by Republicans, who say it would raise taxes and cause financial hardship. Climate change is the significant change in the climate of Earth over a long period of time. It can happen naturally, but today, climate change is largely caused by human activities, including the burning of fossil fuels and clearing of forests.

"Young People Nationwide Are Excited"

Prakash participated in a White House call on September 9 promoting the new job corps.

Prakash and other climate activists have not always supported Biden. They were outraged this spring after Biden approved a huge new oil-drilling project in Alaska, called Willow. For now, though, environmental activists put those concerns aside as they hailed the new jobs program.

The climate corps is modeled after a 1930s program called the Civilian Conservation Corps. It was part of President Franklin D. Roosevelt's famous program known as the New Deal. It created many jobs and helped lift the country out of the Great Depression.

"Young people nationwide are excited to see the launch of the American Climate Corps,″ said Cristina Tzintzún Ramirez. Tzintzún Ramirez is the president of NextGen America, an organization that helps get young people to vote.

"Young people are fighting for climate justice every day in their community," she said. Climate justice is a movement that connects climate issues with human rights issues and takes on both in parallel. "Now they have even more opportunity to continue this fight in their careers," Tzintzún Ramirez added.

A Strong Government Response To Climate Change

More than 50 Democratic lawmakers had also encouraged Biden to create a climate corps. They wrote a letter calling for a strong government response to climate change.

The lawmakers cited recent examples of climate-related disasters, like the deadly heat waves across the nation. They also highlighted the dangerous floods in New England and devastating wildfires in Hawaii.

Democrats called the creation of the climate corps "historic." They said it was a key step toward achieving the vision of the Green New Deal.

Republicans Dismiss The Plan

The White House declined to say how much the program will cost or how it will be paid for. Democrats said money from laws passed in 2021 and 2022 would serve as a "down payment" for thousands of jobs.

Republicans have largely dismissed the climate corps as a proposal that would waste money. They argue that it could even take jobs away from other workers who lost their jobs during the COVID- 19 pandemic.

"We don't need another FDR program," said Arkansas Representative Bruce Westerman in 2021. "The idea that this is going to help land management is a false idea as well."

Similar To State Programs

There are some big differences between the original Civilian Conservation Corps and the new climate corps. For instance, unlike in the 1930s, unemployment is currently low. The new corps is also likely to include people from many backgrounds, unlike the one 90 years ago.

The White House says that the Biden administration will work with at least six different agencies to create the climate corps. It will also work with at least 10 states. California, Colorado, Maine, Michigan and Washington have already begun similar programs, while five more are launching their own climate corps: Arizona, Maryland, Minnesota, North Carolina and Utah.

Many Jobs With One Purpose

The climate corps will provide job training and opportunities to work on a wide range of projects. Some projects are aimed at restoring wet, low-lying coastal areas, known as wetlands. This will help protect communities in those areas from storms and flooding. Other projects will focus on clean energy, like wind and sun. Unlike oil, these are energy sources that do not harm the environment when they are used. Meanwhile, other people will work on managing forests to prevent wildfires and developing energy-efficient solutions to cut people's energy bills.

The creation of the climate corps comes as the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) launches a $4.6 billion grant competition. The grants are meant to help communities cut down their pollution. They are intended to drive community-driven solutions to slow climate change.

The EPA's goal is to help communities "chart their own paths toward the clean energy future."

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: Biden uses executive power to create a New Deal-style American Climate Corps
levels.body:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — After being thwarted by Congress, President Joe Biden will use his executive authority to create a New Deal-style American Climate Corps that will serve as a major green jobs training program.

In an announcement on September 20, 2023, the White House said the program will employ more than 20,000 young adults who will build trails, plant trees, help install solar panels and do other work to boost conservation and help prevent catastrophic wildfires.

The climate corps had been proposed in early versions of the sweeping climate law approved in 2022, but was jettisoned amid strong opposition from Republicans and concerns about cost.

Democrats and environmental advocacy groups never gave up on the plan and pushed Biden in recent weeks to issue an executive order authorizing what the White House now calls the American Climate Corps.

"After years of demonstrating and fighting for a climate corps, we turned a generational rallying cry into a real jobs program that will put a new generation to work stopping the climate crisis,″ said Varshini Prakash, executive director of the Sunrise Movement, an environmental group that has led the push for a climate corps.

With the new corps "and the historic climate investments won by our broader movement, the path toward a Green New Deal is beginning to become visible,″ Prakash said, referring to a comprehensive jobs-and-climate plan supported by many activists and some Democrats but ridiculed by Republicans as a socialist nightmare that would raise taxes and hamper the economy.

Prakash, a frequent Biden critic, participated in a White House call on September 9 promoting the new job corps, which comes as Biden tries to strengthen his appeal to young voters in the 2024 presidential campaign.

The Sunrise Movement and other climate activists, including many young adults, were outraged this spring after Biden approved the huge Willow oil-drilling project in Alaska. Opponents say the project and others approved by Biden put his climate legacy at risk and are a breach of his 2020 campaign promise to stop new oil drilling on federal lands.

Those concerns were put aside, for now, as environmental activists hailed the new jobs program, which is modeled after the Civilian Conservation Corps, created in the 1930s by President Franklin D. Roosevelt, a Democrat, as part of the New Deal.

"Young people nationwide are excited to see the launch of the American Climate Corps, enhancing career pathways in clean energy, conservation and climate resilience,″ said Cristina Tzintzún Ramirez, president of NextGen America, an organization that promotes education, registration and mobilization for voters age 18 to 35.

"Young people are fighting for climate justice every day in their community, and now they have even more opportunity to continue this fight in their careers,″ Ramirez said.

More than 50 Democratic lawmakers, including Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey and New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, had also encouraged Biden to create a climate corps, saying in a letter on September 18 that, "The climate crisis demands a whole-of-government response at an unprecedented scale.″

The lawmakers cited deadly heat waves in the Southwest and across the nation, as well as dangerous floods in New England and devastating wildfires on the Hawaiian island of Maui, among recent examples of climate-related disasters.

Democrats called the creation of the climate corps "historic" and a key step toward fulfilling the vision of the Green New Deal.

"Today President Biden listened to the (environmental) movement, and he delivered with an American Climate Corps,″ a beaming Markey said at a celebratory news conference outside the Capitol.

"We are starting to turn the green dream into a green reality,″ added Ocasio-Cortez, who co-sponsored the Green New Deal legislation with Markey four years ago.

"You all are changing the world,″ she told young activists.

The White House declined to say how much the program will cost or how it will be paid for, but Markey and other Democrats said money from the climate law and the 2021 infrastructure law would serve as a "down payment" for thousands of jobs.

Republicans have largely dismissed the climate corps as a do-gooder proposal that would waste money and could even take jobs away from other workers displaced by the COVID-19 pandemic.

"We don't need another FDR program, and the idea that this is going to help land management is a false idea as well," Arkansas Representative Bruce Westerman, chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee, said in 2021.

Representative Joe Neguse, a Colorado Democrat, said the program should pay "a living wage" while offering health care coverage and other benefits.

A key distinction between the original Civilian Conservation Corps and the new climate contingent is that, unlike the 1930s, the U.S. economy is not in an economic depression. The U.S. unemployment rate was 3.8 percent in August, low by historical measures.

The new corps is also likely to be far more diverse than the largely white and male force created 90 years ago.

White House climate adviser Ali Zaidi said the administration will work with at least six federal agencies to create the climate corps and will pair with at least 10 states. California, Colorado, Maine, Michigan and Washington have already begun similar programs, while five more are launching their own climate corps, Zaidi said: Arizona, Maryland, Minnesota, North Carolina and Utah.

The initiative will provide job training and service opportunities to work on a wide range of projects, including restoring coastal wetlands to protect communities from storm surges and flooding; clean energy projects such as wind and solar power; managing forests to prevent catastrophic wildfires; and energy-efficient solutions to cut energy bills for consumers, the White House said.

The creation of the climate corps comes as the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) launches a $4.6 billion grant competition for states, municipalities and tribes to cut climate pollution and advance environmental justice. The Climate Pollution Reduction Grants are funded by the 2022 climate law and are intended to drive community-driven solutions to slow climate change.

EPA Administrator Michael Regan said the grants will help "communities so they can chart their own paths toward the clean energy future."

The deadline for states and municipalities to apply is April 1, 2024, with grants expected in late 2024. Tribes and territories must apply by May 1, with grants expected by early 2025.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Replacing Dianne Feinstein: Laphonza Butler sworn in as California's newest U.S. senator
levels.body:
Laphonza Butler is California's newest senator. She had a historic swearing-in ceremony with Vice President Kamala Harris in the U.S. Capitol. It took place on October 3, 2023.

Butler raised her right hand to take the oath of office. On either side of her stood California Senator Alex Padilla and Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer. They are both Democrats.

Butler signed her name, and the Senate chamber broke out in applause. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky shook her hand. He is a Republican.

Butler replaces Senator Dianne Feinstein, who recently died. California Governor Gavin Newsom asked Butler to replace Feinstein on October 1. He had previously promised to name a Black woman to the Senate. The Democrats will keep their one-seat majority in the Senate.

Background

Butler is 44 years old. She was never a public official but has worked behind the scenes for Democrats for many years. She worked for Service Employees International Union Local 2015 for more than 10 years. In 2018 she was appointed by then-Governor Jerry Brown to the University of California board. She left in 2021. That same year she became president of Emily's List. The political action committee helps elect Democratic women who support abortion rights.

Butler also worked with Harris during her 2020 bid for president. She did the same for Hillary Clinton in 2016. More recently, she served as an official at Airbnb.

Butler is the first Black woman to serve in the Senate since Harris became vice president. Newsom appointed Padilla to fill Harris's seat. At the time, Padilla was the California Secretary of State. Newsom promised that the next person he appointed would be a Black woman.

Milestones

Butler will be the nation's 12th Black senator. She'll be the third Black woman senator. She is also the first openly gay person of color to serve in the Senate. Moreover, she's the first openly LGBTQ+ person to represent California.

Some Californians wanted Newsom to pick a different Black woman as senator. Supporters and lawmakers wanted U.S. Representative Barbara Lee.

levels.title: A "true trailblazer": Senator Dianne Feinstein of California dies at age 90
levels.body:
Dianne Feinstein was a U.S. lawmaker. She died at age 90.

Feinstein was in the U.S. Senate. She was a Democrat. She was from California, but she died at her home in Washington, D.C. That was on September 28, 2023. On September 29, lawmakers spoke about her. Senator Chuck Schumer said that "we lost a giant in the Senate."

President Joe Biden worked with Feinstein in the Senate. He called her a leader and a friend.

Feinstein was the oldest senator in office. She pushed to protect the environment and limit gun sales. She also reached out to Republicans and found middle ground.

Her death came after health problems kept her away from the Senate. She was out for more than two months earlier in the year.

Praise For Feinstein's Work

On September 29, lawmakers remembered her. The California members of the House of Representatives visited the Senate.

Mitch McConnell is a senator. He is one of the Republicans who praised Feinstein. California and the country are better because of her work, he said.

Biden said, "Dianne made her mark on everything" from the environment to protecting civil rights. The country will see her work for years, he said.

Barack Obama is a former president. He also praised Feinstein as a leader. Former President Bill Clinton called her a champion of civil rights and environmental protection.

She was elected to a San Francisco board of leaders in 1969. San Francisco is in California. She was the first woman to be its board president in 1978. That year, Mayor George Moscone was shot and killed.

San Francisco's First Female Mayor

After Moscone died, Feinstein became the first woman to be the city's mayor. Later, she was one of California's first two women to serve as the state's senators. She also was a leader in Senate groups.

Feinstein had help passing laws because she was good at working with others.

Still, when someone challenged her, she might have a sharp reply. She lost that edge in her later years. Her health was failing.

In February 2023, she said she would not run for office again.

Some of Feinstein's most important work came in 1994. The Senate approved her measure to stop the sales of some kinds of guns. It was part of a bill that Clinton signed into law.

Feinstein was born on June 22, 1933, in San Francisco. She graduated from Stanford University in 1955. In 1980, she married Richard Blum. He died in February 2022.

Feinstein is survived by her daughter, Katherine, and her granddaughter, Eileen. She also has three stepchildren.

levels.title: A "true trailblazer": Senator Dianne Feinstein of California dies at age 90
levels.body:
U.S. lawmaker Dianne Feinstein fought for her causes but also found ways to agree with others. She has died at age 90.

Feinstein was a senator and member of the Democratic Party. Representing California, she died at her home in Washington, D.C., on September 28, 2023. Tributes poured in on September 29. Lawmaker Chuck Schumer, a U.S. Senate leader, announced that "we lost a giant in the Senate."

President Joe Biden served with Feinstein for years in the Senate. He called her "a pioneering American" and a friend.

Feinstein was the oldest sitting U.S. senator. She pushed for causes including environmental protection and gun control. She also was known for reaching out to Republicans and seeking middle ground.

Her death came after health problems sidelined her for more than two months in 2023. Her absence drew frustration, even among her own political group. When she returned to the Senate in May, she voted only occasionally.

Politicians Paid Tribute To Feinstein

On September 29, senators gave tearful tributes. Other lawmakers, the California members of the House of Representatives, stood in the back.

Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell was one of several Republicans who praised Feinstein. "California and our entire nation are better" because of her service, he said.

Biden said, "Dianne made her mark on everything from national security to the environment to protecting civil liberties." The country will benefit from her work for years, he said.

Former President Barack Obama also praised her as a pioneer. Former President Bill Clinton called her a champion of rights, environmental protection and strong national security.

San Francisco's First Female Mayor

Feinstein was elected to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors in 1969. She became its first female board president in 1978. That year, San Francisco Mayor George Moscone was shot and killed alongside another city leader, Harvey Milk. Feinstein found Milk's body.

After Moscone's death, Feinstein became San Francisco's first female mayor. Later, she was one of California's first two female senators. She also was the first woman to head the Senate Intelligence Committee and the first woman to serve as the Senate Judiciary Committee's top Democrat.

Feinstein's experiences shaped her outlook throughout her 50 years in government.

"I recognize that women have had to fight for everything they have gotten, every right," she said in 2005.

Feinstein's efforts to work with Republicans helped her get lawmaking wins.

A fierce debater, she was known for her sharp comebacks when challenged on certain issues. She lost that edge in her later years in the Senate, as her health failed and she sometimes became confused. In February 2023, she said she would not run for a sixth term in the next year. She had stepped down as the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee after the 2020 elections.

Some of Feinstein's most important lawmaking work came in 1994. The Senate approved her measure to stop the manufacturing and sales of some types of assault weapons. It was part of a crime bill that Clinton signed into law. Though the weapons ban ended 10 years later and wasn't replaced, it was an emotional win.

A Historic U.S. Senate Race

In 1990, Feinstein became the first woman picked to run for California governor by a major political party. Although she lost that race, the stage was set for her election to the Senate in 1992.

Feinstein worked with Barbara Boxer, who was running for the state's other U.S. Senate seat, and both won, benefiting from excitement over their historic race. California had never had a female U.S. senator.

Feinstein was born on June 22, 1933, in San Francisco and graduated from college in 1955. In 1980, she married Richard Blum. He died in February 2022.

Feinstein is survived by her daughter, Katherine, and her granddaughter, Eileen. She also has three stepchildren.

levels.title: A "true trailblazer": Senator Dianne Feinstein of California dies at age 90
levels.body:
Elected to the U.S. Senate in 1992, Dianne Feinstein fought for her causes but also found paths to agreements with others. She has died at age 90.

Feinstein, a Democrat from California, died September 28, 2023, at her home in Washington, D.C., her office said September 29. Tributes poured in all day. Senator Chuck Schumer, a Senate leader, announced that "we lost a giant in the Senate."

As the nation feels "this tremendous loss, we know how many lives she impacted," Schumer said.

President Joe Biden, who served with Feinstein for years in the Senate, called her "a pioneering American" and a "cherished friend."

Feinstein was the oldest sitting U.S. senator, pushing for priorities including environmental protection, reproductive rights and gun control. She was also known for reaching out to the opposing political party of Republicans and seeking middle ground.

Her death came after health problems including shingles sidelined her for more than two months earlier in 2023. Her absence drew frustration and brought an unsuccessful attempt by Democrats to temporarily replace her on the Senate Judiciary Committee. When she returned to the Senate in May, she voted only occasionally.

Politicians Paid Tribute To Feinstein

On September 29, her Senate desk was draped in black and topped with a vase of white roses. Senators gave tearful tributes as California members of the House of Representatives stood in the back. Representative Nancy Pelosi sat with Feinstein's daughter, Katherine.

Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell was one of several Republicans who gave tributes to Feinstein. "Her beloved home state of California and our entire nation are better" because of her service, he said.

Biden said in a statement, "Dianne made her mark on everything from national security to the environment to protecting civil liberties." The country will benefit from her work "for generations," he said.

Former President Barack Obama also saluted her as a pioneer. Former President Bill Clinton called her a champion "of civil rights and civil liberties, environmental protection and strong national security."

San Francisco's First Female Mayor

Feinstein was elected to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors in 1969 and became its first female board president in 1978. That year, San Francisco Mayor George Moscone was gunned down alongside Supervisor Harvey Milk at City Hall by a disgruntled former supervisor. Feinstein found Milk's body.

After Moscone's death, Feinstein became San Francisco's first female mayor. Later, she was one of California's first two female senators, the first woman to head the Senate Intelligence Committee and the first woman to serve as the Senate Judiciary Committee's top Democrat.

Feinstein's experiences colored her outlook throughout her five decades in politics.

"I recognize that women have had to fight for everything they have gotten, every right," she said in 2005.

Feinstein's efforts to work with Republicans helped her notch legislative wins throughout her career.

A fierce debater, the California senator was known for her sharp comebacks when challenged on issues she cared about. She lost that edge in her later years in the Senate, as her health declined and she sometimes became confused when speaking publicly. In February 2023, she said she would not run for a sixth term the next year. She had stepped down as the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee after the 2020 elections.

A Historic U.S. Senate Race

One of Feinstein's most significant legislative accomplishments was early in her career. The Senate approved her amendment to ban the manufacturing and sales of certain types of assault weapons. It was part of a crime bill that Clinton signed into law in 1994. Though the assault weapons ban ended 10 years later and wasn't renewed, it was an emotional win after her experience with gun violence.

In 1990, she won the Democratic nomination for California governor and was the first female major-party nominee for the office.

Although she lost the election to Republican Pete Wilson, the stage was set for her election to the Senate.

Feinstein campaigned with Barbara Boxer, who was running for the state's other U.S. Senate seat, and both won, benefiting from excitement over their historic race. California had never had a female U.S. senator.

During Donald Trump's presidency, Feinstein became the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee in 2016 and led her party's messaging through three U.S. Supreme Court nominations.

Confirmation Hearings Caused Controversy

Feinstein closed out confirmation hearings for Justice Amy Coney Barrett by hugging and thanking Judiciary Committee Chair Lindsey Graham. He is a Republican from South Carolina. She called the hearings some of the best she's participated in.

Liberal groups opposed having Barrett replace the late liberal icon Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. Barrett is considered conservative, with Republicans supporting her. Some called for Feinstein to step down from committee leadership. Later, she announced she would remain on the committee, but step down as the top Democrat.

Feinstein was born on June 22, 1933, in San Francisco and graduated from Stanford University in 1955, with a bachelor's degree in history. In 1980, she married Richard Blum, who died in February 2022.

In addition to her daughter, Feinstein has a granddaughter, Eileen, and three stepchildren.

levels.title: A "true trailblazer": Senator Dianne Feinstein of California dies at age 90
levels.body:
A champion of liberal causes who was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1992 and broke gender barriers throughout her career, Dianne Feinstein has died at age 90.

Feinstein, a Democrat from California, died September 28, 2023, at her home in Washington, D.C., her office said September 29. Tributes poured in all day. Opening the Senate floor, Majority Leader Chuck Schumer announced that "we lost a giant in the Senate."

"As the nation mourns this tremendous loss, we know how many lives she impacted and how many glass ceilings she shattered along the way," Schumer said.

President Joe Biden, who served with Feinstein for years in the Senate, called her "a pioneering American" and a "cherished friend."

Feinstein was the oldest sitting U.S. senator and an advocate for liberal priorities important to her state, including environmental protection, reproductive rights and gun control. However, she was also known as a practical lawmaker who reached out to Republicans and sought middle ground.

Politicians Paid Tribute To Feinstein

Her death came after a bout of shingles sidelined her for more than two months earlier in 2023. Her absence drew frustration and launched an unsuccessful attempt by Democrats to temporarily replace her on the Senate Judiciary Committee. When she returned to the Senate in May, she voted only occasionally.

On September 29, her Senate desk was draped in black and topped with a vase of white roses. Senators gave tearful tributes as members of the California House delegation stood in the back of the chamber and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi sat with Feinstein's daughter, Katherine.

Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell was one of several Republicans who gave tributes to the Democratic icon. "Her beloved home state of California and our entire nation are better for her dogged advocacy and diligent service," he said.

Biden said in a statement, "Dianne made her mark on everything from national security to the environment to protecting civil liberties. Our country will benefit from her legacy for generations."

Former President Barack Obama also saluted her as a pioneer. Former President Bill Clinton called her a champion "of civil rights and civil liberties, environmental protection and strong national security."

San Francisco's First Female Mayor

She was elected to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors in 1969 and became its first female board president in 1978. That year San Francisco Mayor George Moscone was gunned down alongside Supervisor Harvey Milk at City Hall by Dan White, a disgruntled former supervisor. Feinstein found Milk's body.

After Moscone's death, Feinstein became San Francisco's first female mayor. Later, she was one of California's first two female senators, the first woman to head the Senate Intelligence Committee and the first woman to serve as the Senate Judiciary Committee's top Democrat.

Feinstein's experiences colored her outlook throughout her five decades in politics.

"I recognize that women have had to fight for everything they have gotten, every right," she said in 2005.

Feinstein's bipartisan efforts helped her notch legislative wins throughout her career. However, it also proved to be a liability in her later years in Congress, as her state became more liberal and as the Senate and voters became increasingly polarized.

A fierce debater, the California senator was long known for her sharp comebacks when challenged on issues she felt strongly about. She lost that edge in her later years in the Senate, as her health declined and she sometimes became confused when answering questions or speaking publicly. In February 2023, she said she would not run for a sixth term the next year.

Amid the concerns about her health, Feinstein stepped down as the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee after the 2020 elections.

A Historic U.S. Senate Race

One of Feinstein's most significant legislative accomplishments was early in her career, when the Senate approved her amendment to ban the manufacturing and sales of certain types of assault weapons. It was part of a crime bill that Clinton signed into law in 1994. Though the assault weapons ban expired 10 years later and wasn't renewed or replaced, it was an emotional win after her experience with gun violence.

In 1990, she won the Democratic nomination for California governor and was the first female major-party gubernatorial nominee in the state.

Although she narrowly lost the general election to Republican Pete Wilson, the stage was set for her election to the Senate two years later.

Feinstein campaigned jointly with Barbara Boxer, who was running for the state's other U.S. Senate seat, and both won, benefiting from excitement over their historic race. California had never had a female U.S. senator, and female candidates and voters had been stirred up by the U.S. Supreme Court hearings in which the all-male Senate Judiciary Committee questioned Anita Hill about her sexual harassment statements against nominee Clarence Thomas.

During Donald Trump's presidency, Feinstein became the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee in 2016 and led her party's messaging through three U.S. Supreme Court nominations.

Confirmation Hearings Caused Controversy

Feinstein closed out confirmation hearings for Justice Amy Coney Barrett with an embrace of Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Lindsey Graham, a Republican from South Carolina, and a public thanks to him. "This has been one of the best set of hearings that I've participated in," Feinstein said at the end of the hearings.

Liberal advocacy groups that had opposed Barrett's nomination to replace the late liberal icon Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg were furious. They called for her to step down from the committee leadership.

Later, Feinstein announced she would remain on the committee, but step down as the top Democrat.

Feinstein was born on June 22, 1933, in San Francisco and graduated from Stanford University in 1955. In 1980, she married investment banker Richard Blum, who died in February 2022, and thanks to his wealth, she was one of the richest members of the Senate.

In addition to her daughter, Feinstein has a granddaughter, Eileen, and three stepchildren.

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: A "true trailblazer": Senator Dianne Feinstein of California dies at age 90
levels.body:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Dianne Feinstein of California, a centrist Democrat and champion of liberal causes who was elected to the Senate in 1992 and broke gender barriers throughout her long career in local and national politics, has died. She was 90.

Feinstein died on September 28, 2023, at her home in Washington, D.C., her office said on September 29. Tributes poured in all day. Opening the Senate floor, Majority Leader Chuck Schumer announced that "we lost a giant in the Senate."

"As the nation mourns this tremendous loss, we know how many lives she impacted and how many glass ceilings she shattered along the way," Schumer said, his voice cracking.

President Joe Biden, who served with Feinstein for years in the Senate, called her "a pioneering American," a "true trailblazer" and a "cherished friend."

Feinstein, the oldest sitting U.S. senator, was a passionate advocate for liberal priorities important to her state — including environmental protection, reproductive rights and gun control — but was also known as a pragmatic lawmaker who reached out to Republicans and sought middle ground.

Her death came after a bout of shingles sidelined her for more than two months earlier this year — an absence that drew frustration from her most liberal critics and launched an unsuccessful attempt by Democrats to temporarily replace her on the Senate Judiciary Committee. When she returned to the Senate in May, she was frail and using a wheelchair, voting only occasionally.

On September 29, her Senate desk was draped in black and topped with a vase of white roses. Senators gave tearful tributes as members of the California House delegation stood in the back of the chamber and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi sat in the gallery with Feinstein's daughter, Katherine.

Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell was one of several Republicans who gave tributes to the Democratic icon, calling her his friend. "Dianne was a trailblazer, and her beloved home state of California and our entire nation are better for her dogged advocacy and diligent service," McConnell said.

Biden said in a statement, "Dianne made her mark on everything from national security to the environment to protecting civil liberties. "Our country will benefit from her legacy for generations."

Former President Barack Obama also saluted her as "a trailblazer," and former President Bill Clinton called her a champion "of civil rights and civil liberties, environmental protection and strong national security."

She was elected to the San Francisco (California) Board of Supervisors in 1969 and became its first female board president in 1978, the year San Francisco Mayor George Moscone was gunned down alongside Supervisor Harvey Milk at City Hall by Dan White, a disgruntled former supervisor. Feinstein found Milk's body.

After Moscone's death, Feinstein became San Francisco's first female mayor. In the Senate, she was one of California's first two female senators, the first woman to head the Senate Intelligence Committee and the first woman to serve as the Judiciary Committee's top Democrat.

Although Feinstein was not always embraced by the feminist movement, her experiences colored her outlook throughout her five decades in politics.

"I recognize that women have had to fight for everything they have gotten, every right," she told The Associated Press in 2005, as the Judiciary Committee prepared to hold hearings on President George W. Bush's nomination of John Roberts to replace Sandra Day O'Connor on the U.S. Supreme Court.

"So I must tell you, I try to look out for women's rights. I also try to solve problems as I perceive them, with legislation, and reaching out where I can, and working across the aisle," she said.

Feinstein's bipartisan efforts helped her notch legislative wins throughout her career. But it also proved to be a liability in her later years in Congress, as her state became more liberal and as the Senate and the electorate became increasingly polarized.

A fierce debater who did not suffer fools, the California senator was long known for her verbal zingers and sharp comebacks when challenged on the issues about which she was most fervent. But she lost that edge in her later years in the Senate, as her health visibly declined and she sometimes became confused when answering questions or speaking publicly. In February 2023, she said she would not run for a sixth term the next year. And within weeks of that announcement, she was absent from the Senate for more than two months as she recovered from a bout of shingles.

Amid the concerns about her health, Feinstein stepped down as the top Democrat on the judiciary panel after the 2020 elections, just as her party was about to take the majority. In 2023, she said she would not serve as the Senate president pro tempore, or the most senior member of the majority party, even though she was in line to do so. The president pro tempore opens the Senate every day and holds other ceremonial duties.

One of Feinstein's most significant legislative accomplishments was early in her career, when the Senate approved her amendment to ban the manufacturing and sales of certain types of assault weapons as part of a crime bill that former President Clinton signed into law in 1994. Though the assault weapons ban expired 10 years later and was never renewed or replaced, it was a poignant win after her career had been significantly shaped by gun violence.

Feinstein became mayor of San Francisco after the 1978 slayings of Moscone and Milk, leading the city during one of the most turbulent periods in its history. Even her critics credited Feinstein with a calming influence, and she won reelection on her own to two four-year terms.

With her success and growing recognition statewide came visibility on the national political stage.

In 1984, Feinstein was viewed as a vice presidential possibility for Walter Mondale, but faced questions about the business dealings of her husband, Richard Blum. In 1990, she used news footage of her announcement of the assassinations of Moscone and Milk in a television ad that helped her win the Democratic nomination for California governor, making her the first female major-party gubernatorial nominee in the state's history.

Although she narrowly lost the general election to Republican Pete Wilson, the stage was set for her election to the Senate two years later to fill the Senate seat Wilson had vacated to run for governor.

Feinstein campaigned jointly with Barbara Boxer, who was running for the state's other U.S. Senate seat, and both won, benefiting from positive news coverage and excitement over their historic race. California had never had a female U.S.

senator, and female candidates and voters had been galvanized by the U.S. Supreme Court hearings in which the all-male Senate Judiciary Committee questioned Anita Hill about her sexual harassment allegations against nominee Clarence Thomas.

Feinstein was appointed to the judiciary panel and eventually the Senate Intelligence Committee, becoming the chairperson in 2009. She was the first woman to lead the intelligence panel, a high-profile perch that gave her a central oversight role over U.S. intelligence controversies, setbacks and triumphs, from the killing of Osama bin Laden to leaks about National Security Agency surveillance.

Under Feinstein's leadership, the intelligence committee conducted a wide-ranging, five-year investigation into CIA interrogation techniques during President George W. Bush's administration, including waterboarding of terrorism suspects at secret overseas prisons. The resulting 6,300-page "torture report" concluded among other things that waterboarding and other "enhanced interrogation techniques" did not provide key evidence in the hunt for bin Laden. A 525-page executive summary was released in late 2014, but the rest of the report has remained classified.

The Senate investigation was full of intrigue at the time, including documents that mysteriously disappeared and accusations traded between the Senate and the CIA that the other was stealing information. The drama was captured in a 2019 movie about the investigation called "The Report," and actor Annette Bening was nominated for a Golden Globe for her portrayal of Feinstein.

In the years since, Feinstein has continued to push aggressively for eventual declassification of the report.

"It's my very strong belief that one day this report should be declassified," Feinstein said. "This must be a lesson learned: that torture doesn't work."

During Donald Trump's presidency, Feinstein became the top Democrat on the judiciary panel in 2016 and led her party's messaging through three U.S. Supreme Court nominations.

Feinstein closed out confirmation hearings for Justice Amy Coney Barrett with an embrace of Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Lindsey Graham, a Republican from South Carolina, and a public thanks to him for a job well done. "This has been one of the best set of hearings that I've participated in," Feinstein said at the end of the hearings.

Liberal advocacy groups that had fiercely opposed Barrett's nomination to replace the late liberal icon Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg were furious and called for her to step down from the committee leadership.

A month later, Feinstein announced she would remain on the committee, but step down as the top Democrat. The senator, then 87 years old, did not say why. In a statement, she said she would "continue to do my utmost to bring about positive change in the coming years."

Feinstein was born on June 22, 1933, in San Francisco. She graduated from Stanford University in 1955, with a bachelor's degree in history. In 1980, she married investment banker Richard Blum, and thanks to his wealth, she was one of the richest members of the Senate. He died in February 2022.

In addition to her daughter, Feinstein has a granddaughter, Eileen, and three stepchildren.
