cover.caption: NASA astronaut Frank Rubio is expected to spend 371 days in orbit, making him the first American to spend more than a year in space on a single mission.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: "It was unexpected": NASA astronaut breaks U.S. record for longest single spaceflight
levels.body:
Frank Rubio is a NASA astronaut. He was supposed to spend six months in space. Instead, he stayed for more than a year.

Rubio was living on the International Space Station (ISS). The ISS is a laboratory. It circles the Earth. It is where astronauts from around the world live and learn about space.

On September 11, Rubio broke a NASA record. He completed the longest single space flight. The previous record was 355 days. On September 27, Rubio touched down on Earth. He logged a total of 371 days on the ISS.

On the ISS, Rubio had problems with his spacecraft. A spacecraft is a vehicle or machine. It is built to work in harsh environments. This includes outer space.

Rubio was only supposed to be in space for six months. But the spacecraft issues forced him to stay longer.

"It was unexpected. In some ways, it's been an incredible challenge," Rubio said. "But in other ways, it's been an incredible blessing."

Coolant Leak Caused Delay

Rubio traveled to the ISS on a Russian spacecraft. It is called the MS-22 Soyuz. He flew with Sergey Prokopyev and Dmitri Petelin. They both work with Roscosmos. This is the Russian space agency.

MS-22 was meant to be their ride home. Then, in December 2022, something happened. The spacecraft lost all of its coolant during a leak. Coolant is a liquid or gas. It is used to remove heat from something.

So Roscosmos shipped up an empty replacement spacecraft. It is called MS-23. It arrived at the ISS in February 2023.

But Rubio and his crewmates still had to wait for a relief crew. The relief crew was supposed to use MS-23. That meant they needed a new spacecraft. They were reassigned to MS-24. Their departure was delayed to September 15.

Finally, on September 27, Rubio and his two crewmates left the ISS. They flew on board the MS- 23. They touched down to Earth safely. They parachuted into Kazakhstan.

The Tomato That Got Away

Rubio said that the NASA community rallied around him. They made sure his family was doing well while he was in space. NASA recently upgraded the internet on the ISS. So Rubio was able to have video calls with family.

Rubio's crew grew tomatoes in space. But Rubio did not get to eat his tomato. It floated away. He hopes someone finds it someday.

"I spent so many hours looking for that thing," he said. But he never found it.

Only seven astronauts have spent more than a year in space. The other four were Russian astronauts on missions visiting the then-Soviet Mir space station.

NASA astronaut Frank Rubio (left) and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Prokopyev (center) and Dmitri Petelin (right) prepare for their MS-22 Soyuz spacecraft launch in September 2022.
As part of an experiment to see how plants grow in outer space, Frank Rubio tends to Arabidopsis seedlings in Plant Habitat-03 at the International Space Station in July 2023.

levels.title: "It was unexpected": NASA astronaut breaks U.S. record for longest single spaceflight
levels.body:
NASA astronaut Frank Rubio was supposed to spend six months in space. Instead, he stayed for more than a year.

Rubio was living on the International Space Station (ISS). The ISS is a laboratory that circles the Earth. It is where astronauts from around the world live and learn about space.

Rubio broke NASA's record for the longest single space flight on September 11. The previous record was 355 days. And on September 27, Rubio touched down to Earth, logging a total of 371 days on the ISS. This made Rubio the first American to spend more than a year in space on a single mission.

Rubio spent twice as long in space as he was supposed to. Problems with his spacecraft forced a six-month stay to double to a year. A spacecraft is a vehicle or machine. it is specially designed and built to work in harsh environments such as outer space.

"It was unexpected. In some ways, it's been an incredible challenge," Rubio said. "But in other ways, it's been an incredible blessing."

Coolant Leak Caused Delay

Rubio is a Salvadorian American. His record-breaking stay falls during National Hispanic Heritage Month, which concludes October 15. He finds it timely because he said it "symbolizes the diversity of the wonderful rich fabric of America."

In September 2022, Rubio launched to the ISS. He traveled with his Russian crewmates Sergey Prokopyev and Dmitri Petelin. They made the journey on the MS-22 Soyuz spacecraft. Prokopyev and Petelin both work with Roscosmos, the Russian space agency.

Both Rubio and Petelin were on their first flight to the ISS.

The MS-22 spacecraft was meant to provide their ride home as well. But then, in December 2022, the spacecraft lost all of its coolant during a leak. Coolant is a liquid or gas that is used to remove heat from something. So Roscosmos shipped up an empty replacement spacecraft, called MS-23. It arrived to the ISS in February 2023.

But Rubio and his crewmates still had to wait for a relief crew. The relief crew was supposed to use MS-23. That meant they needed a new spacecraft. They were reassigned to MS-24. Their departure was delayed to September 15.

Finally, on September 27, Rubio and his two crewmates touched down to Earth safely. They parachuted to a landing in Kazakhstan aboard the MS-23.

The Tomato That Got Away

Rubio said that the NASA community rallied around him. They made sure his family was doing well while he was in space. And luckily, NASA recently upgraded the internet on the ISS. Rubio was able to have video calls with family at least twice a week.

Rubio joked that his only regret was not eating one of the tomatoes his crew grew in space. Rubio's tomato floated away before he could take a bite.

"I spent so many hours looking for that thing," he said. But he never found it.

Only seven astronauts have spent more than a year in space. The other four were Russian astronauts on missions visiting the then-Soviet Mir space station.

Rubio broke the 355-day record last set by NASA astronaut Mark Vande Hei. In early September, Vande Hei spoke with Rubio. Vande Hei said the most memorable part of his own stay was "the people that I got to spend that much time [with] … intensively, both working and playing as much as we possibly can."

NASA astronaut Frank Rubio celebrated a spaceflight milestone with two former astronauts on Earth.

Rubio spoke with senior NASA management from the International Space Station (ISS) on September 13, 2023, two days after breaking the previous record of 355 days on a single spaceflight.

On September 27, Rubio touched back down to Earth, logging a total of 371 days in orbit, making him the first American to spend more than a year in space on a single mission. More incredibly, it wasn't planned that way; problems with his spacecraft forced an expected six-month orbital stay to double to a year.

"It was unexpected. In some ways, it's been an incredible challenge," Rubio said of the milestone during the livestreamed call on NASA Television, with NASA Administrator Bill Nelson and Deputy Administrator Pam Melroy. "But in other ways, it's been an incredible blessing. I count myself lucky and honored to be able to represent the agency and our country."

Rubio, a Salvadorian American born in Los Angeles, California, added that with his record-breaking stay falling during National Hispanic Heritage Month (which concludes October 15), he finds it "timely" as it "symbolizes the diversity of the wonderful rich fabric of America."

Rubio and his Russian MS-22 Soyuz spacecraft crewmates Sergey Prokopyev and Dmitri Petelin, cosmonauts from Roscosmos, were scheduled to spend a typical six months in space after launching on September 21, 2022. Both Rubio and Petelin were on their first flight.

Halfway through their stay, however, MS-22, also serving as their ride home, dramatically lost all its coolant in a December 2022 leak. After considering options, Roscosmos rapidly shipped up an empty replacement Soyuz, called MS-23, which arrived on February 25, 2023.

The agencies also formulated an emergency escape plan from the ISS before MS-23 arrived, assigning Rubio to a temporary seat (involving tie-down straps on the floor of an already docked SpaceX Crew Dragon). His Russian crewmates were authorized to use MS-22 if absolutely needed, as two humans would not heat up the uncooled spacecraft as rapidly as three. But that plan luckily did not need to be implemented after MS-23 safely docked.

Rubio and his crewmates, however, were needed to stay on board until a relief crew could arrive. That required getting yet another spacecraft (MS-24) ready for spaceflight to send the astronauts. Since NASA astronaut Loral O'Hara and Roscosmos cosmonauts Oleg Kononenko and Nikolai Chub were supposed to use MS-23, that crew's departure date on MS-24 was delayed to no earlier than September 15 for their MS-24 reassignment.

On September 27, Rubio, Petelin and Prokopyev touched down to Earth safely, parachuting to a landing in Kazakhstan aboard the MS-23.

"As much as it was a challenge to stay an extra six months, I'm so grateful that the agency was able to say, 'Hey, you know what the safe thing to do would be: To fire up a new spacecraft, and have [my crew] wait and ensure a more safe return,'" Rubio said in the call, adding, "I am looking forward to a return on a more safe and more secure spacecraft."

Nelson and Melroy, both flown astronauts from the space shuttle program, paid tribute to the challenges Rubio had faced in orbit. (Melroy flew three times as a NASA astronaut. Nelson, then a member of the House of Representatives on a space committee, flew on mission STS-61C in 1986 under a program NASA then had for nonprofessionals to reach space.)

"You made all kinds of records up there, and you've had six months that you didn't expect," said Nelson, speaking from NASA's headquarters in Washington, D.C.

Melroy, standing beside Nelson in the view of the video, said Rubio's wife and kids "have been on my mind so much." The former astronaut added she wanted to check in to make sure Rubio was getting the support he needed.

Rubio said that the NASA community had rallied around him, sending people over to the house as needed to help the family. Luckily, upgrades to NASA's internet on station came in during his mission as well, allowing for high-quality video conferences with family at least twice a week, he said.

Rubio joked that his only regret was not eating one of the space-grown Red Robin tomatoes his crew tended, and managed to save from an unexpected humidity drop on ISS at a crucial growth point. Rubio's inch-long tomato unfortunately floated away to a hidden spot before he could take a bite. "I spent so many hours looking for that thing," he quipped. "I'm sure the desiccated tomato will show up at some point and vindicate me, years in the future."

Only seven astronauts have spent more than a year in space. Aside from the trio on MS-22/23, the other four were cosmonauts on missions visiting the then-Soviet Mir space station. Topping the list is Valery Polyakov (437 days), while the others are Sergey Avdeev, Musa Manarov and Vladimir Titov.

Rubio's mark surpasses the 355-day record last set by NASA astronaut Mark Vande Hei. Vande Hei was also expected to spend six months in space, but learned preflight that he might extend to a year due to space station staffing needs (which is what ended up happening).

Vande Hei, speaking with Rubio in early September from NASA's Johnson Space Station in Houston, Texas, said the most memorable part of his own stay was "the people that I got to spend that much time [with] … intensively, both working and playing as much as we possibly can."

title: Should AI help Georgia students write college admissions essays?
zhTitle: AI 该不该帮学生写大学申请文书

cover.caption: With more students relying on ChatGPT to write their essays, colleges such as Georgia Tech set some guidelines for their applicants.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Should AI help Georgia students write college admissions essays?
levels.body:
Many high school seniors are applying to colleges. Some have to write admissions essays. They may get help from ChatGPT.

ChatGPT is a software system. It writes code. It also generates text. It can produce essays and stories. ChatGPT is powered by artificial intelligence (AI). AI is an approach that uses code to teach a machine to spot patterns and make decisions. The company OpenAI created ChatGPT. The company released ChatGPT as a free web-based tool in 2022.

Some professors fear that ChatGPT could lead to cheating. Others think that ChatGPT could help students. Now, college admissions offices must weigh in. Georgia Tech is one of the first schools to issue guidance around AI.

Brainstorming Is OK

Many schools have said nothing about using AI for college applications, said Rick Clark. He works at Georgia Tech. Clark is in charge of undergraduate admissions.

Georgia Tech says applicants can use ChatGPT. They can use it to brainstorm. They can use it for editing. But they shouldn't copy and paste paragraphs. According to Georgia Tech, "Your ultimate submission should be your own."

Riley Samples goes to Seckinger High School. It is in Buford, Georgia. Samples is a senior there. She is working on 15 admissions essays. She uses AI to check grammar.

She said AI is not good at writing with personality. "It's very flat," she said.

Ethical Concerns

Noelle Halverson is a senior at Seckinger, too. A teacher encouraged her to use ChatGPT for creative writing. Halverson used it to flesh out plot details. But using it for applications feels wrong to her, she said.

Lauren Chiru-Danzer is a junior at Seckinger. She used ChatGPT to research law schools. She thinks it's ethical to use AI as "a way to get ideas started." But copying AI text is plagiarism, she said.

"That's Not Really My Voice"

Many students get stuck on essays. Clark said admissions departments should do what they can to "de-stress the process." ChatGPT can help students, he said.

"It gets them … started, thinking about things, and then realizing, 'Well, that's not exactly the way I want to put it. Or, that's not really my voice,'" he said.

Admissions officers are also using AI. Georgia Tech plans to run its applications through a computer program. They want to see how the program will score them. They will compare the scores from humans to the ones from computers. But people will still decide which students get in.

"That's Not Really My Voice"

For first-generation students and others who don't have access to college coaching, AI might help make the application process fairer, Clark said.

"It gets them throwing out some stuff, getting started, thinking about things and then realizing, 'Well, that's not exactly the way I want to put it. Or, that's not really my voice,'" he said.

Admissions officers are exploring how AI could work for them, too.

Last year, humans read more than 52,000 undergraduate applications to Georgia Tech. This year, the school plans to run applications through a computer program, too. Officials will check how the program scores submissions compared to humans. But ultimately, people will still decide which students get in.

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: Should AI help Georgia students write college admissions essays?
levels.body:
Thousands of high school seniors applying to one of Georgia's most selective universities are tackling the same admissions essay question: "Why do you want to study your chosen major specifically at Georgia Tech?"

The best writers will respond with authenticity, personality, a solid grasp of grammar and maybe a dash of wit. Some even will consult ChatGPT for help.

And that's just fine with Georgia Tech, to a point. The highly ranked public research school in Atlanta is among the first to issue guidance about how to use artificial intelligence (AI) as the applicants write their essays.

ChatGPT upended classrooms when it launched last fall, forcing professors to contend with a new cheating threat and figure out how to incorporate it into courses. Now, the disruption is pounding at the admissions office door.

There's been "deafening silence" from many schools about the use of AI in college applications, said Rick Clark, Georgia Tech's executive director of undergraduate admission. That was all the more reason to tackle it head on as applications for fall 2024 admission opened August 1, 2023.

Georgia Tech applicants can use a chatbot to brainstorm essay ideas, organize their thoughts and edit. But they shouldn't copy and paste AI-authored paragraphs into their applications. According to Georgia Tech, "Your ultimate submission should be your own."

"We know students are using it in their own academic work in high school, and so if they're going to, let's give them … some guardrails," Clark said.

The AI conundrum adds to the upheaval happening as some competitive colleges adjust policies following the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in late June to end race-conscious admissions programs.

Elite institutions have taken varied approaches. The University of Michigan Law School tells applicants to write all drafts and the final product, declaring they "ought not use ChatGPT or other artificial intelligence tools." Duke University pointed to guidelines developed to assist faculty as they think about the use of AI in classrooms, but the recommendations don't specifically address admissions.

The Common Application, accepted by 1,000 schools including roughly two dozen in Georgia, advises colleges "to set reasonable parameters" around the use of AI, said Jenny Rickard, the organization's president and CEO, in a written statement. Just over half of Common App schools don't require an essay.

One in 10 high school seniors and incoming college freshmen used or likely will use ChatGPT to write their college application essays, according to a recent survey of about 750 students by the online site Intelligent. Nearly all students who used AI to write their essays said the text it produced "required some or a lot of editing," the survey found.

Riley Samples, a senior at Seckinger High School in Gwinnett County, is working on 15 essays as she applies to about seven colleges, including Georgia Tech and some in the Ivy League. The submissions will vary from short statements to 800-word pieces.

Samples thought it was interesting Georgia Tech didn't ban AI entirely but steered applicants away from plagiarizing. She errs on the side of caution, using such programs only to check grammar.

"I think AI-generated essays cannot really capture who you are as a person," Samples said. "When it writes, it's very flat. It's not very emotion-filled."

Campus Policies

Georgia Tech, the University of Georgia (UGA) and the private Oglethorpe University in Brookhaven are among those addressing how to use AI in applications.

UGA advises those seeking admission to treat AI programs "like any other form of assistance, whether it is a parent, counselor or friend," but the writing must be the applicant's own.

Oglethorpe recognizes AI as a "powerful and convenient" tool that can assist with "language, grammar and structure" in an essay or application. But, the school stresses, "Ultimately, we want to learn about you from you."

Rebecca Sandidge, Oglethorpe's vice president for enrollment management, said it's too hard to police the use of AI.

"My goal is to not villainize AI," she said. "It is a tool and students have to learn how to use it appropriately."

Detection tools are unreliable, Clark said. Ultimately, the best way to deter students from submitting all-bot essays is to remind them that the writing won't impress admissions readers.

Georgia College & State University hasn't provided applicants with specific guidance regarding AI, a spokeswoman said. Neither has the private Emory University, though a spokeswoman said, "We expect applicants to write their essays themselves."

Spelman College also doesn't have a policy forbidding the use of AI in admissions essays. Ingrid Hayes, senior vice president for enrollment management, said in a statement that if AI-generated text is suspected, it "may raise doubts about the students' academic potential in the holistic application review."

Abby Hyken, a senior at Atlanta's Midtown High School who plans to apply to about a dozen colleges, has used ChatGPT to brainstorm debate team arguments, where it provided a helpful starting point. But the text it generates is emotionless and "not that good." She has not turned to it for the 20 or more college essays on her to-do list.

Hyken's biggest writing challenge is showcasing her personality and how she'd fit into a school "without sounding too cliche."

Ethical Concerns

At Seckinger High School, a school that intertwines artificial intelligence into courses, students are accustomed to thinking about its ethical uses.

Noelle Halverson, a senior, experimented with ChatGPT when a teacher encouraged her class to try it on a creative writing assignment. Halverson used it to flesh out plot details and to look for a period-appropriate name for an 18th century character.

Using a chatbot to help with college essays, though, doesn't feel right, she said. "It wouldn't be me at all."

The college search is "a daunting task," said Seckinger junior Lauren Chiru-Danzer, who has used ChatGPT to research schools in the Northeast with good law programs.

"We are constantly discussing the ethical implications of AI," she said. "We have deemed it ethical to use AI as almost like a brainstorming partner, as a way to get ideas started. But it is not ethical to copy and paste what AI has given to you because it is plagiarism."

College counselors at the Buckhead-based Access Test Prep & Tutoring help students brainstorm ideas for essays, edit and proofread. Co-founder Elaine Rosenblum said teenagers communicate in smartphone "text-speak" and learn formulaic writing in high school. But those skills don't exactly translate into crafting strong college essays, which should capture a student's personality and a reader's attention.

So far, AI writing can't replicate nuance and emotion, said Rosenblum. Relying on ChatGPT is "a very dangerous proposition" unless colleges clearly state what's allowed.

"I wouldn't test the waters," she said. "I think it's lazy. It's the opposite of what a college wants you to do. Why risk it?"

Rosenblum draws a distinction between students who use AI and those who hire advisers to help them apply to college.

"Someone who is doing college counseling that has integrity will not write the essay for the student," she said.

"Paralysis Of The Blinking Cursor"

For first-generation students or those from rural communities who don't have access to college coaching, AI isn't an equalizer, but it might help democratize the application process, Clark said. Georgia Tech's guidance notes that "AI could be a helpful collaborator, particularly when you do not have access to other assistance to help you complete your application."

And while essays are a valuable component of a student's application, it's exceedingly rare to admit or deny someone based on those writings, Clark said. Grades, academic rigor, test scores and involvement outside of class are critical to decision-makers, he said.

Still, many students get stuck on essays. Clark calls it the "paralysis of the blinking cursor" and said admissions departments should do what they can to "de-stress the process." That's where ChatGPT can chip in.

"It gets them throwing out some stuff, getting started, thinking about things and then realizing, 'Well, that's not exactly the way I want to put it. Or, that's not really my voice,'" he said.

Students aren't the only ones figuring out how to use AI. Admissions officers are exploring how it could work for them, too.

Last year, humans read more than 52,000 undergraduate applications to Georgia Tech. They'll do so again this year (2023), but the school is testing the use of AI in its own process. The school plans to run applications through a computer program at the end of the admissions cycle. Officials will check how the program scores submissions compared to humans, who will still decide who gets in, Clark said.

"We have to find ways to learn and to be more efficient and to spend our time on what really matters," he said.

title: Twelve-year-old becomes national golf champ after playing only three full rounds
zhTitle: 只打过三轮完整比赛的全国冠军
reason: 一名十二岁自闭症球员夺冠，报道写了他的训练方式与家庭支持。

cover.caption: After only playing three rounds of golf, golfer Bayleigh Teepa-Tarau wins the nine-hole title at the Zespri AIMS Games in Tauranga, New Zealand. His teacher, Whetu Wiremu (right), introduced Bayleigh to the sport.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Twelve-year-old becomes national golf champ after playing only three full rounds
levels.body:
Twelve-year-old Bayleigh Teepa-Tarau won a major New Zealand golf contest. Bayleigh has autism. His autism means he sometimes has trouble communicating with others. But it doesn't stop him from being good at golf. In fact, it may even help. Before winning the contest, Bayleigh had only played three full rounds of golf in his life.

Bayleigh played in the Association of Intermediate and Middle Schools (AIMS) Games. The AIMS Games are New Zealand's biggest sporting event for 11- to 13-year-olds. Bayleigh won the gold medal in nine-hole golf. He played with borrowed clubs. He doesn't even own a set of clubs.

Bayleigh didn't just win a gold medal. He also helped his school win the team title. His performance was incredible. It was particularly incredible for someone who has been playing for such a short time.

"Bayleigh is just unbelievable and has natural talent," said Mickey Huriwaka. He is a longtime golfer. He said watching Bayleigh was like watching a pro golfer. "That was how good he was."

Borrowed Clubs And Three Rounds Of Practice

Whetu Wiremu is Bayleigh's golf coach. He is a teacher's aide at the Tāneatua School. He recently started a golf team at the school. Someone told him Bayleigh used to carry around a golf stick. So, Wiremu asked the quiet boy if he wanted to join the team.

Bayleigh said, "OK."

The children took group lessons for six months, Wiremu said. But they weren't able to learn much. He said the boys never got "one-on-one kind of help."

The school didn't have enough money to buy golf clubs for Bayleigh and his teammates. Instead, Wiremu had to borrow clubs. He drove the kids to a nearby golf course. They played three full rounds of practice. Each round lasted around three hours.

"He doesn't worry about if he's done a bad shot or a good shot," Wiremu said of Bayleigh. "He just loves the sport." It's that love that makes him so good, Wiremu added.

"I Want To Be Like Tiger Woods"

Wiremu believes Bayleigh's autism helped him during the contest. It helped him focus on the game.

"I just treat him like a normal kid," Wiremu added. "So I just … talk to Bayleigh and treat him like his friends."

Bayleigh's autism may have played a role in his keeping calm and unbothered by bad shots, Wiremu said.

"He doesn't really get nervous for anything that he does. He kind of just does it to have fun. And if he wins or does a good job in it, then that's just a bonus," Wiremu said.

Bayleigh lives in Tāneatua, a working-class town of fewer than 1,000 residents on the northern coast of the North Island. Bayleigh has become a local celebrity after the AIMS win, his coach and friends say. A local business said it would buy Bayleigh and his teammates their own set of golf clubs. Golf New Zealand, the nation's governing body for golf, has reached out to the school and offered golfing equipment and clothing for the students.

To celebrate their success, Wiremu took Bayleigh and his teammates to have sushi, Bayleigh's favorite food. After that, Bayleigh suggested that they go to a driving range to play more golf.

"I like playing golf, and I'm always going to play golf," Bayleigh said when asked about his dream job. "I want to be like Tiger Woods."

title: What to know about the latest Israel-Hamas conflict
zhTitle: 以色列与哈马斯冲突：背景说明
reason: 封锁、控制权与历次战争，读懂新闻标题需要的那条时间线。

cover.caption: Palestinians (left) walk amid the rubble following Israeli airstrikes that razed swaths of a neighborhood in Gaza City on October 10, 2023. At right, Israeli police officers evacuate a family from a site in Ashkelon that was hit by a rocket fired from the Gaza Strip on October 7, 2023.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: What to know about the latest Israel-Hamas conflict
levels.body:
October 7, 2023, was a major Jewish holiday. On that day, Hamas militants from Gaza made a surprise attack on Israel. The militants killed and kidnapped many people. In response, Israel launched rockets into Gaza. Israel's Prime Minister said the country is now at war with Hamas.

Hamas has been in power in Gaza for 16 years. The U.S. State Department considers Hamas to be a terrorist group. The European Union and other Western countries also consider it a terrorist organization.

Hamas attacked as many as 22 locations in Israel. They gunned down civilians and soldiers.

Israel's military said on October 10 that it had regained control over its border with the Gaza Strip. Its government vowed to hunt down the militants.

The conflict already has killed people on both sides. More than 1,000 people have died in Israel, and 830 people have been killed in Gaza and the West Bank.

More than 150 people were kidnapped by Hamas. The hostages are Israeli soldiers, women, children, and the elderly. Some of the hostages are from other countries. Hamas says it will kill a hostage every time Israel's military bombs civilian targets in Gaza without warning.

A Narrow Coastal Strip

Gaza is just 25 miles long and six miles wide. At 139 square miles, it's about the same size as Detroit, Michigan.

Over 2 million Palestinians live in Gaza. It is part of a region called the Southern Levant. The area has been called many names, including Palestine, Israel, and Canaan. Both Jews and Arabs, many of whom are Muslim, have historical and indigenous ties to the region.

In 1948, the area was under British control. The United Nations decided that the territory would be split into two countries. Palestine would be Arab, while Israel would be Jewish. Israel declared its independence and Arab countries invaded, starting the 1948 Arab-Israeli War.

Many Palestinians fled or were forced to leave. Egypt captured Gaza during the fighting. Jordan took control of two other Palestinian areas — East Jerusalem and the West Bank.

In 1967, Israel and its neighbors went to war again. This time, Israel captured Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem.

The first Palestinian intifada, or uprising, began in Gaza in 1987. It later spread to the West Bank and East Jerusalem. Hamas emerged in Gaza during this time. In the 1990s an agreement with Israel created a Palestinian government called the Palestinian Authority, which was given partial control over Gaza and the West Bank.

The Hamas Takeover

A second intifada happened in 2005. Israel withdrew from Gaza.

In 2006, Hamas won the Palestinian elections. Hamas clashed with the Palestinian Authority, and then took control of Gaza.

In 2007, Egypt and Israel closed their borders with Gaza. This blockade has lasted 16 years.

The Blockade

Israel says the blockade keeps Hamas and other militant groups from importing weapons. Egypt says it wants to stop the conflict from spilling over into its borders. Rights groups say the blockade punishes all Gazans.

Gaza is a hard place to live. About half of the Gazans don't have jobs, electricity goes out frequently and the tap water is polluted.

Palestinians in Gaza cannot leave the territory without permission. This makes it extremely difficult to leave the country to work, study or visit family.

The Wars

Hamas and Israel have fought three wars and several smaller battles.

In 2021, an 11-day war between Israel and Hamas began after a dispute at the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, a site sacred to both Jews and Muslims.

Israel's military has destroyed Gazan neighborhoods, forcing thousands to makeshift shelters.

Hamas has fired thousands of rockets into Israel, creating widespread fear. Their range has steadily increased in recent years.

Why Now?

In recent years, Israel has made peace deals with Arab countries. In the past, Arab countries didn't want to make peace with Israel. The U.S. has recently been trying to make a deal between Israel and Saudi Arabia. Hamas receives support from Iran. Iran is Saudi Arabia's enemy.

Meanwhile, Israel has a new far-right government. Its politicians support Israeli settlements in the Palestinian West Bank. Palestinians and the United Nations consider those settlements to be illegal.

Israeli religious nationalists have also increased their visits to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. Recently, hundreds of ultra-Orthodox Jews and Israeli activists visited the site. This angered Hamas. For decades there had been an agreement. Muslims were allowed to pray there, but not Jews.

Hamas leaders say there are several reasons for the attack. They include an Israeli crackdown on militants in the West Bank and the settlements. They also cite thousands of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Israel's blockade of Gaza.

At right, Israeli police officers evacuate a family from a site in Ashkelon that was hit by a rocket fired from the Gaza Strip on October 7, 2023.
figures.credit: Photos: Fatima Shbair and Tsafrir Abayov/AP

During the major Jewish holiday of Simchat Torah on October 7, 2023, Hamas militants from Gaza fired a barrage of rockets and stormed into Israeli towns. The militants killed dozens and abducted others in an unprecedented surprise attack. Israel launched retaliatory airstrikes in Gaza. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the country is now at war with Hamas.

Hamas has been in power in Gaza since 2007. The U.S. State Department designated Hamas a terrorist group in 1997. The European Union and other Western countries also consider it a terrorist organization.

Hamas gunmen attacked as many as 22 locations outside of the Gaza border. The militants reached as far as 15 miles (24 kilometers) inside of Israel. In some places, they gunned down civilians and soldiers.

Israel's military said on October 10 that it had regained control over its border with the Gaza Strip.

The Israeli government vowed to hunt down the militants and to attack Gaza, the Palestinian territory ruled by Hamas and home to 2 million people.

The conflict already has killed hundreds on both sides. More than 1,000 people have died in Israel, and 830 people have been killed in Gaza and the West Bank.

Israel says it tries to avoid civilian casualties when it targets Hamas sites. But Hamas militants also fire rockets and operate in civilian areas. Israel accuses them of using civilians for cover while drawing return fire to houses, offices and mosques.

The families of more than 150 people kidnapped by Hamas feared for the lives of their loved ones. The hostages include Israeli soldiers, women, children, and the elderly, along with dozens of foreigners. Hamas has threatened to kill one of the hostages every time Israel's military bombs civilian targets in Gaza without warning.

A Narrow Coastal Strip

Gaza is a Palestinian territory sandwiched between Israel and Egypt, and just 25 miles long and six miles wide. At 139 square miles, it's about the same size as Detroit, Michigan.

Gaza is home to over 2 million Palestinians. It is part of the Southern Levant, a region that has had many names throughout history, including Palestine, Israel, and Canaan. Both Jews and Arabs, many of whom are Muslim, have historical and indigenous ties to the region.

In 1948, the United Nations (U.N.) decided that the territory, then under British control, would be split into two countries. Palestine would be Arab, while Israel would be Jewish. Nearby Arab countries did not agree with this. Israel declared its independence and Arab countries invaded, starting what is now known as the 1948 Arab-Israeli War.

Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians fled the fighting or were forced to leave. Egypt captured Gaza during the fighting. Jordan took control of two other Palestinian areas — East Jerusalem and the West Bank.

Israel captured Gaza, along with the West Bank and East Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war. The Palestinians want all three territories to form their future Palestinian nation.

The first Palestinian intifada, or uprising, began in Gaza in 1987, later spreading to the West Bank and East Jerusalem. Hamas emerged in Gaza during the first intifada. The Oslo peace process in the 1990s established a Palestinian government called the Palestinian Authority (PA). The PA was given partial control over Gaza and the West Bank.

The Hamas Takeover

A second, more violent intifada happened in 2005. Israel withdrew from Gaza.

The following year, Hamas won the Palestinian elections. That triggered a power struggle with the Palestinian Authority that left Hamas in control of Gaza.

Hamas has been known to arrest political opponents and suppress protests against its rule.

In 2007, Egypt and Israel closed their borders with Gaza. This blockade has lasted 16 years.

The Blockade

Israel says the blockade is needed to keep Hamas and other militant groups from importing weapons. Egypt maintains the blockade to prevent Hamas-related conflict from spilling over into its borders. Rights groups say the blockade punishes all Gazans.

The closures, along with years of Hamas' misrule, have devastated Gaza's economy. Unemployment is around 50 percent, power outages are frequent and the tap water is polluted.

Movement restrictions make it difficult for Palestinians in Gaza to travel abroad for work, study or to visit family. They often refer to Gaza as the world's largest open-air prison.

The Wars

Hamas and Israel have fought three wars and several smaller battles. The worst so far was the 2014 war, when 2,200 Palestinians and 73 Israelis were killed.

In 2021, there was a dispute at the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, a site sacred to both Jews and Muslims. This led to a bloody 11-day war.

Israel's military has destroyed entire Gazan neighborhoods, forcing thousands to makeshift shelters.

Hamas has fired thousands of rockets into Israel, sowing widespread fear and bringing life to a standstill. Their range has steadily increased in recent years, with some striking as far as the major cities of Tel Aviv and Jerusalem.

Why Now?

In recent years, Israel has made peace deals with Arab countries. In the past, Arab countries were unwilling to make peace with Israel without agreements to aid Palestinians. The U.S. has recently been trying to broker a deal between Israel and Saudi Arabia. Hamas receives support from Saudi Arabia's enemy, Iran.

Meanwhile, Israel has a new far-right government, which supports the continuation of Israeli settlements in the Palestinian West Bank. Palestinians and the United Nations consider those settlements to be illegal.

Israeli religious nationalists have also increased their visits to the Temple Mount compound in Jerusalem. Recently, during the Jewish harvest festival of Sukkot, hundreds of ultra-Orthodox Jews and Israeli activists visited the site. Palestinians accused Jews of praying there, a violation of an agreement between the two governments.

Hamas leaders say an Israeli crackdown on militants in the West Bank, its settlements, its imprisonments of Palestinians in Israeli jails, and its blockade of Gaza pushed it to attack.

At right, Israeli police officers evacuate a family from a site in Ashkelon that was hit by a rocket fired from the Gaza Strip on October 7, 2023.
figures.credit: Photos: Fatima Shbair and Tsafrir Abayov/AP

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: What to know about the latest Israel-Hamas conflict
levels.body:
Backed by a barrage of rockets, Hamas militants stormed from the blockaded Gaza Strip into nearby Israeli towns, killing dozens and abducting others in an unprecedented surprise attack during a major Jewish holiday on October 7, 2023. A stunned Israel launched airstrikes in Gaza, with its prime minister saying the country is now at war with Hamas and vowing to inflict an "unprecedented price."

Hamas has been in power in Gaza since 2007. The U.S. State Department designated Hamas a terrorist group in 1997. The European Union and other Western countries also consider it a terrorist organization.

In an assault of startling breadth, Hamas gunmen rolled into as many as 22 locations outside the Gaza Strip, including towns and other communities as far as 15 miles (24 kilometers) from the Gaza border. In some places, they gunned down civilians and soldiers as Israel's military scrambled to muster a response.

Israel's military said on October 10 that it had regained effective control over its south and the border with the Gaza Strip.

The declaration came as the Israeli Defense Forces sought to make good on the government's vow to hunt down the militants and to intensify an assault on densely populated Gaza, the Palestinian territory ruled by Hamas and home to 2 million people.

The conflict already has killed hundreds on both sides. The Israeli military said more than 1,000 people have died in Israel since the incursion on October 7. In Gaza and the West Bank, 830 people have been killed, according to authorities there.

Israel says it takes pains to avoid civilian casualties as it targets Hamas sites in Gaza, which is heavily built up and has scant open space. But Hamas militants also fire rockets and operate in civilian areas, using civilians for cover while drawing return fire to houses, offices and mosques.

In Israel and beyond, the families of more than 150 people kidnapped by Hamas and other militant groups feared for the lives of their loved ones. The armed wing of Hamas has warned it will kill one of the hostages every time Israel's military bombs civilian targets in Gaza without warning.

The latest eruption of violence raised the specter of another devastating war and once again drew international attention to the impoverished, densely populated strip.

Here's a look at the Gaza Strip and its place in the Middle East conflict.

A Narrow Coastal Strip

Gaza, sandwiched between Israel and Egypt, is just 25 miles (40 kilometers) long and 6 miles (10 kilometers) wide. It was part of the British-ruled Palestine Mandate before the 1948 Arab- Israeli War. After the war, Gaza came under Egypt's control.

Large numbers of Palestinians who fled or were driven from what is now Israel during that war ended up in Gaza, and the refugees and their descendants now number 1.4 million, accounting for more than half of Gaza's population.

Israel captured Gaza, along with the West Bank and East Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war. The Palestinians want all three territories to form their future state.

The first Palestinian intifada, or uprising, erupted in Gaza in 1987 — the same year Hamas was founded — and later spread to the other occupied territories. The Oslo peace process in the 1990s established the Palestinian Authority and gave it limited autonomy in Gaza and parts of the occupied West Bank.

The Hamas Takeover

Israel withdrew its troops and Jewish settlements from Gaza in 2005, after a second and far more violent intifada.

The following year, Hamas won a landslide victory in the Palestinian elections. That triggered a power struggle with Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' Fatah party, culminating in a week of clashes in 2007 that left Hamas in control of Gaza.

Hamas has done little in the way of imposing Islamic law on Gaza, which was already very conservative. But it has shown no tolerance for dissent, arresting political opponents and violently suppressing rare protests against its rule.

The militant group has remained firmly in power through three wars and a 16-year blockade.

The Blockade

Israel and Egypt imposed the crippling blockade after the Hamas takeover. Israel says it's needed to keep Hamas and other militant groups from importing arms. Rights groups say the blockade is a form of collective punishment.

The closures, along with years of misrule and Hamas' long-running feud with the Palestinian Authority, have devastated Gaza's economy. Unemployment hovers at around 50 percent, power outages are frequent and the tap water is badly polluted.

Palestinians face heavy movement restrictions that make it difficult to travel abroad for work, study or to visit family, and often refer to Gaza as the world's largest open-air prison.

The Wars

Hamas and Israel have fought three wars and several smaller battles. The worst so far was the 2014 war, which lasted for 50 days and killed some 2,200 Palestinians, more than half of them civilians. Seventy-three people were killed on the Israeli side.

Then in 2021, a dispute at the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, sacred to both Muslims and Jews, and which includes the Al-Aqsa Mosque, spilled over into a bloody 11-day war between Israel and Hamas.

Israel's airstrikes and incursions into Gaza have left vast swaths of destruction, with entire neighborhoods reduced to rubble and thousands forced to shelter in United Nations schools and other facilities. Israel says it makes every effort to avoid civilian casualties and accuses Hamas of using Gazans as human shields.

Palestinian militants have fired thousands of rockets into Israel. The vast majority are intercepted by Israeli missile defenses or land in open areas, but they sow widespread fear and can bring life to a standstill. Their range has steadily increased in recent years, with some striking as far as Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, major metropolitan areas.

Why Now?

In recent years, Israel has made peace deals with Arab countries without having to make concessions in its conflict with the Palestinians. The U.S. has recently been trying to broker a deal between Israel and Saudi Arabia, a bitter rival of Hamas' Iranian backers.

Meanwhile, Israel's new far-right government was working to cement Israeli settlements in the West Bank despite Palestinian opposition.

Hamas officials cited long-simmering tensions, including competing claims over the Temple Mount site. In recent years, Israeli religious nationalists — such as Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister — have increased their visits to the Temple Mount compound. Recently, during the Jewish harvest festival of Sukkot, hundreds of ultra-Orthodox Jews and Israeli activists visited the site, prompting condemnation from Hamas and accusations that Jews were praying there in violation of the status quo agreement.

Hamas leaders say an Israeli crackdown on militants in the West Bank, continued construction of settlements — which the international community considers to be illegal — thousands of prisoners in Israeli jails, and its ongoing blockade of Gaza pushed it to attack.

Its leaders say hundreds of its 40,000 fighters took part in the assault. Israel says the group has about 30,000 fighters and an arsenal of rockets, including some with a range of about 250 kilometers (155 miles), and unmanned drones.

title: "A Million Miles Away" tells story of Latino migrant worker turned NASA astronaut
zhTitle: 从农场工人到 NASA 航天员
reason: 一部传记片背后的真实履历，以及电影改写掉的部分。

cover.caption: NASA astronaut José Hernández waits to enter the space shuttle discovery at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida on August 7, 2009. Since he was a young child, he set the goal of becoming an astronaut.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: "A Million Miles Away" tells story of Latino migrant worker turned NASA astronaut
levels.body:
José Hernández grew up working in the California fields. He was a migrant farmworker with his family. When he was 10 years old he realized he wanted to be an astronaut.

In 1972, Hernández was watching the last Apollo mission on television. He remembers watching men walk on the moon in black-and-white. He went outside and looked up at the moon. That's when he knew he wanted to be an astronaut.

Hernández made that dream come true. He became a NASA astronaut. He is also an engineer. An engineer is a person who invents, designs, tests, and builds systems, processes, and products to solve problems.

A movie about Hernández is now streaming on Amazon Prime. It is called "A Million Miles Away." It follows Hernández and his family. They traveled from a rural village in Mexico to the fields of California. The movie then follows Hernández's journey all the way to the International Space Station (ISS). The ISS is a laboratory that circles the Earth. It is where astronauts from around the world live and learn about space.

A Family Effort

Hernández said he did not go from being a migrant farmworker to being an astronaut on his own. He had a lot of help. He said the movie did a good job showing this.

Everyone pitched in. His parents stopped moving from field to field. They put their dream of building a home back in Mexico on the back burner. Hernández's wife also put her dream of opening a restaurant on hold. She did this so Hernández could focus on NASA.

Hard Work Pays Off

NASA picked Hernández for astronaut training in May 2004. He had been turned down 11 times before that.

"I felt I had done the work and the preparation,'" Hernández said. But he knew he might not get picked. Around 12,000 people applied for 15 spots.

"But I still thought, 'It's about time.' Because I felt so ready many cycles before," he said.

He completed training in 2006. His mission launched into orbit in 2009.

Hernández doesn't just want viewers to feel inspired. He wants to help them put their dreams into action.

"It's worth dreaming big, as long as you're willing to put in the work and effort," Hernández said. "There's a recipe there, sprinkled throughout the movie. It's an inspirational movie but you also have some tools to take home with you."

figures.credit: Photo: NASA/Jim Grossmann Photo: NASA/Jim Grossmannu/Strongu

levels.title: "A Million Miles Away" tells story of Latino migrant worker turned NASA astronaut
levels.body:
José Hernández first dreamt of becoming an astronaut when he was 10 years old. He worked the California fields as a migrant farmworker with his family. He remembers staring up at the sky on a cold December night in 1972.

"I was watching the very last Apollo mission, kneeling down in front of a black-and-white TV," said engineer and former NASA astronaut Hernández. An engineer is a person who invents, designs, tests, and builds systems, processes, and products to solve problems.

"Then I went outside and I saw the moon, almost full, came back and heard the reporter Walter Cronkite narrate that whole moonwalk," Hernández said. That's when he knew he wanted to be an astronaut.

Hernández fulfilled that dream. In 2009, he was assigned to the crew of the space shuttle mission STS-128.

A movie based on Hernández's memoir is now streaming on Amazon Prime. It is called "A Million Miles Away." It follows Hernández and his family from a rural village in Mexico to the fields of California, and all the way to the International Space Station. The ISS is a laboratory that circles the Earth. It is where astronauts from around the world live and learn about space.

Making A Movie — And Dreams — Come True

"A Million Miles Away" stars actor Michael Peña as Hernández. The actress Rosa Salazar plays Hernández's wife. The film was directed and co-written by Mexican filmmaker Alejandra Márquez Abella.

Hernández said the film did a great job of representing his story. "It wasn't just a story about one individual rising as a migrant farmworker to become a U.S. NASA astronaut but rather a community effort," he said.

Everyone made sacrifices to help Hernández reach his dream. His parents stopped moving from field to field and put their dream of building a home back in Mexico on the back burner. His wife put her dream of opening a restaurant on hold so Hernández could focus on NASA. Hernández even missed the birth of one of his children, which is portrayed in a gut-wrenching scene in the movie.

The former NASA astronaut and director knew they wanted Peña to take the lead.

"He's such a hardworking and impressive actor," Márquez Abella said. "It amazes me how he is on set and how he prepares for his scenes. His conviction, strength and work ethic are admirable."

Hard Work Pays Off

NASA selected Hernández for astronaut training in May 2004. He had been turned down 11 times before that.

"I felt I had done the work and the preparation to finally get selected but you have to understand over 12,000 people apply for 10-15 positions so the competition is very stiff," Hernández said.

In February 2006, he completed astronaut candidate training. His training included scientific and technical briefings, physiological training, flight training, and water and wilderness survival training. He then worked on various technical assignments. In July 2008, he was selected as a mission specialist. That mission launched into orbit the following fall.

Hernández doesn't just want viewers watching his story to feel inspired. He wants to help them put their dreams into action.

"It's worth dreaming big, as long as you're willing to put in the work and effort to convert that dream into reality," Hernández said. "There's a recipe there, sprinkled throughout the movie. The tools are there. It's an inspirational movie but you also have some tools to take home with you."

Hernández said the film did a "masterful job at representing my story and ensuring that it wasn't just a story about one individual rising as a migrant farmworker to become a U.S. NASA astronaut but rather a community effort."

Everyone in Hernández's circle made sacrifices to help him reach his dream. His parents stopped moving him and his siblings from field to field and put their dream of building a home back in Mexico on the back burner, and his wife put her dream of opening a restaurant on hold so Hernández could focus on NASA. Hernández even missed the birth of one of his children, which is portrayed in a gut-wrenching scene in the movie.

When it came to casting for Hernández's role, the former NASA astronaut and director Márquez Abella knew they wanted Peña to take the lead.

It was the middle of the pandemic when Peña accepted the role, but Hernández said he and Peña met virtually and connected right away.

"He's such a hardworking and impressive actor," Márquez Abella said. "It amazes me how he is on set and how he prepares for his scenes. His conviction, strength and work ethic are admirable."

Hard Work Pays Off

Hernández was turned down 11 times for astronaut training by NASA before being selected in May 2004.

"I felt I had done the work and the preparation to finally get selected but you have to understand over 12,000 people apply for 10-15 positions so the competition is very stiff," Hernández said about the process. "But I still thought, 'It's about time.' Because I felt so ready many cycles before."

In February 2006, he completed astronaut candidate training that included scientific and technical briefings, physiological training, flight training, and water and wilderness survival training. He then worked on various technical assignments until his selection in July 2008 as a mission specialist, and he launched to the ISS the following fall.

Hernández wants viewers watching his story to not only feel inspired but also walk away with the tools necessary to put their dreams into action.

"It's worth dreaming big, as long as you're willing to put in the work and effort to convert that dream into reality," Hernández said. "There's a recipe there, sprinkled throughout the movie. The tools are there. It's an inspirational movie but you also have some tools to take home with you."

levels.title: "A Million Miles Away" tells story of Latino migrant worker turned NASA astronaut
levels.body:
It was a cold December night in 1972 when a 10-year-old boy who worked the fields as a migrant farmworker with his family looked up at the sky and dreamed of becoming an astronaut.

"I was watching the very last Apollo mission, kneeling down in front of a black-and-white TV, hanging on to the rabbit ear antennas to improve the reception watching Gene Cernan walking the moon," engineer and former NASA astronaut José Hernández tells USA Today. "Then I went outside and I saw the moon, almost full, came back and heard the reporter Walter Cronkite narrate that whole moonwalk. That's when I was hooked. 'That's it,' I said, 'I want to be like that guy.'"

He fulfilled that dream in 2009 when he was assigned to the crew of the space shuttle mission STS-128.

Inspired by the NASA flight engineer's real-life story and based on Hernández's memoir, the Amazon Prime Video biopic "A Million Miles Away" on its streaming service follows him and his family of proud migrant workers on a decades-long journey, from a rural village in Michoacán, Mexico, to the fields of the San Joaquin Valley, California, to more than 200 miles above the Earth in the International Space Station.

Starring actor Michael Peña, from "Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan" and "Martian," as a soft-spoken and determined Hernández and Rosa Salazar, from "Brand New Cherry Flavor" and "Bird Box," as Hernández's sharp-witted and supportive wife, "A Million Miles Away" is the embodiment of the saying, "It takes a village."

After all, it was a family affair reaching his goal, Hernández says.

Directed and co-written by Mexican filmmaker Alejandra Márquez Abella, whose credits include "Northern Skies Over Empty Space" and "The Good Girls," the film did a "masterful job at representing my story and ensuring that it wasn't just a story about one individual rising as a migrant farmworker to become a U.S. NASA astronaut but rather a community effort," Hernández adds.

Everyone in Hernández's circle made sacrifices to help him reach his dream. His parents stopped moving him and his siblings from field to field and put on the backburner their dream of building a home back in Mexico. His wife put her dream of opening a restaurant on hold so Hernández could focus on NASA, and while he's preparing for his future, in a gut-wrenching scene, Hernández also misses the birth of one of his children.

"It was my family's effort, my wife's contribution — everything," Hernández says.

When it came to casting for Hernández's role, the former NASA astronaut and director Márquez Abella knew they wanted Peña to take the lead.

It was the middle of the pandemic when he accepted the role, but Hernández says he and Peña connected virtually and he "got the gist of my personality, my sense of humor and that coupled with his trips with Alejandra to NASA ... it was a natural choice. He did a masterful job."

"Michael is a superstar; there was no other option," Márquez Abella says.

"He's such a hardworking and impressive actor," she adds. "It amazes me how he is on set and how he prepares for his scenes. His conviction, strength and work ethic are admirable."

But if it's not a pandemic, it's a strike as the director and real-life subject of "A Million Miles Away" promote the film without their leading stars.

"It's sad that when Michael gets a nice leading role, and Rosa, too, that they can't be here to enjoy the fruits of their labor," Hernández says. "I'm trying to do the best I can to represent them now since they represented me on screen."

He then worked on various technical assignments until his selection in July 2008 as a mission specialist which launched into orbit the following fall.

Hernández wants viewers watching his story to not only feel inspired but also walk away with the tools necessary to put their dreams into action.

"It's worth dreaming big, as long as you're willing to put in the work and effort to convert that dream into reality," Hernández says. "There's a recipe there, sprinkled throughout the movie. The tools are there. It's an inspirational movie but you also have some tools to take home with you."

title: Thrift store shopper discovers lost painting by N.C. Wyeth
zhTitle: 旧货店里认出的失踪画作
reason: 一次辨认怎样被证实，艺术品鉴定要走的几道程序。

cover.caption: A woman bought this painting for $4 at a thrift store in Manchester, New Hampshire. It turned out to be a valuable work of art by the painter N.C. Wyeth.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Thrift store shopper discovers lost painting by N.C. Wyeth
levels.body:
Earlier this year, a woman went shopping for a picture frame. She came out of the store with buried treasure.

The woman went to the Savers thrift store in Manchester, New Hampshire. She dug in a pile of frames and pulled a painting. She bought it for just $4.

Art experts think the painting was created by N.C. Wyeth. He is an American painter. N.C. Wyeth is famous for his portraits and landscapes. He also made paintings to go in the book "Treasure Island."

This discovery is probably his painting "Ramona." It shows a daughter and her foster mother. It is part of a series that went with a book that was also called "Ramona." The book was written in 1884 by Helen Hunt Jackson.

The drawings or paintings that go with a book are called illustrations. The illustrated version of "Ramona" came out in 1939. Wyeth made four paintings to go with the book. Two of the others are still lost.

Many of Wyeth's paintings have sold for a lot of money. Some have even sold for millions of dollars. In September 2023, the woman sold the painting for $191,000.

"Lost" Painting Hung In Private Home For Years

After woman first bought the painting, she hung it in her home. One day, she posted a picture of it on Facebook. People online were excited. They told her that it might be painted by a famous artist.

The woman went to the Brandywine Museum of Art. They have the largest collection of Wyeth paintings. She also met with Lauren Lewis. Lewis is an expert on Wyeth's work in particular. Lewis thought the painting could be real.

Bonhams Skinner is the company that sold the painting. Experts at Bonhams Skinner examined the painting. They said that it was real, too. It had the same kind of frame and backing that Wyeth used to use.

Nobody knows how the painting ended up in a thrift store. Bonhams Skinner workers have a theory. Maybe someone connected to the book version of "Ramona" received it as a gift. It might also have been given to Helen Hunt Jackson.

Kathleen Leland works at Bonhams Skinner. She says that discoveries like this one are rare. You probably won't find a rare painting the next time you go to the thrift store. So don't be too hard on yourself!

levels.name: 基础
levels.title: Thrift store shopper discovers lost painting by N.C. Wyeth
levels.body:
Earlier this year, a woman was shopping for a picture frame at the Savers thrift store in Manchester, New Hampshire. But, she did not find one.

The painting she pulled out of a mismatched pile of frames at a New Hampshire thrift store turned out to be a long-lost 1930s work by American painter N.C. Wyeth of Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania.

The woman bought what is now believed to be N.C. Wyeth's work "Ramona"from Savers for a mere $4. It sold for $191,000 at an auction run by the company Bonhams Skinner.

"Lost" Painting Hung In Private Home For Years

The woman remembers how she felt when she pulled it out of the pile of frames. In that moment, she joked that she had maybe found something valuable. Bonhams spokeswoman Sheri Middleton said that the woman's discovery has been "a bit overwhelming for her." She also said that the woman prefers not to have her name released to the media.

The woman decided to hang the painting in her home. She never thought that it was the work of one of America's best painters. When she searched for it on the Internet, she didn't find anything resembling the painting.

N.C. Wyeth's works are distinctive. The works he created from his Chadds Ford studio were known all over the world. He also famously illustrated an edition of the novel "Treasure Island." He lived between 1882 and 1945 and was the father of American master painter Andrew Wyeth.

This piece is one of four Wyeth created for Helen Hunt Jackson's 1884 book "Ramona." The book was released with the paintings in 1939. In it, a determined orphan faces her unforgiving foster mother.

The painting stayed in the woman's home for years until she decided to post it on a Facebook group called "Things found in Walls." That's when things got interesting.

Strangers Told Her She Might Have Treasure

Some commenters in the Facebook group recognized the painting as a possible N.C. Wyeth. They sent the woman to the Brandywine Museum of Art in Chadds Ford. They also connected her to a former Wyeth curator in Maine named Lauren Lewis.

Lewis drove three hours to meet the woman, who noticed how excited Lewis was. That was the first time the woman began to realize that the painting might be real.

Painting Fetches Hundreds Of Thousands At Auction

Bonhams Skinner is the company that sold the painting. It was sold at an auction, where people competed to take home the painting by offering the highest price. Some of Wyeth's more famous workshave sold for millions of dollars. Bonhams predicted that the painting would fetch between $150,000 and $250,000. It sold for $191,000.

One of Bonhams Skinner's employees told the woman that the painting was likely real. How did they know? First, it matched Wyeth's signature style. Also, it was placed in a simple frame with a red panel in the back. Both of these were details common to Wyeth's work.

The largest known collection of N.C. Wyeth works is held by the Brandywine Museum of Art. It also offers tours of the artist's Chadds Ford home and studio. Only one of the other three illustrations from the "Ramona" book is known to have been recovered.

It's still not known how the painting ended up in a thrift store. Bonhams Skinner has one theory. They suspect that book publisher Little, Brown and Company gifted it. It might have gone to one of "Ramona'"s editors or ended up with the author's belongings after she died.

Thrift-store lovers shouldn't get their hopes up they'll find lost paintings, said Leland. She said that discoveries like this one are uncommon.

levels.name: 进阶
levels.title: Thrift store shopper discovers lost painting by N.C. Wyeth
levels.body:
The woman wasn't shopping for fine art at the Savers thrift store in Manchester, New Hampshire. She was looking for a nice frame that she could put a different picture in.

Instead, she made a life-changing discovery: The painting she pulled out of a mismatched pile of frames at a New Hampshire thrift store turned out to be a long-lost 1930s work by American master N.C. Wyeth of Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania.

The woman bought what is now believed to be N.C. Wyeth's work "Ramona" from Savers for a mere $4. It sold for $191,000 at a September 19, 2023, auction run by the company Bonhams Skinner.

"Lost" Painting Hung In Private Home For Years

The woman remembered joking that she had maybe found something valuable when she pulled it out of the pile of frames. Bonhams spokeswoman Sheri Middleton said that the woman's discovery has been "a bit overwhelming for her." She also said that the woman prefers not to have her name released to the media.

The woman decided to hang it in her home, never suspecting it was the work of a well-known American painter. When she searched for it on the Internet, she didn't find anything resembling the painting.

N.C. Wyeth's works are quite distinctive. The works he created from his Chadds Ford studio a were known around the world. He also famously illustrated an edition of the novel "Treasure Island." He lived between 1882 and 1945 and was the father of American master painter Andrew Wyeth.

This piece is one of four Wyeth created for a 1939 edition of Helen Hunt Jackson's 1884 book "Ramona." It depicts the tense relationship between an orphan and her unforgiving foster mother. The painting stayed in the woman's home for years until she decided to post it on a Facebook group called "Things found in Walls." That's when things got interesting.

Strangers Told Her She Might Have Treasure

Some commenters in the Facebook group recognized the painting as a possible N.C. Wyeth. They sent the woman to the Brandywine Museum of Art in Chadds Ford. They also connected her to a former Wyeth curator in Maine named Lauren Lewis.

Lewis drove three hours to meet the woman, who noticed how excited Lewis was. That was the first time when the woman began to realize that the painting might be real.

Experts at auction house Bonhams Skinner confirmed that the painting was likely an original. First, it matched Wyeth's signature style. It also was placed in the practical frame and backing panel that Wyeth was known to use.

"Beginning in the mid-1930s, Wyeth used a particular type of artist board: Weber 'Renaissance' panels, distinctive for their red backs and elaborate labels. And this was the case for this painting," auction house expert Kathleen Leland told art blog Hyperallergic this month.

Painting Fetches Hundreds Of Thousands At Auction

Some of Wyeth's better-known works, such as "Portrait of a Farmer,"have sold for millions of dollars at auction. The company had expected the painting to fetch anywhere between $150,000 and $250,000. It ended up selling for $191,000.

The largest known collection of N.C. Wyeth works is held by the Brandywine Museum of Art, which also offers tours of the artist's Chadds Ford home and studio. Only one of the other three illustrations from the "Ramona" book is known to have been recovered.

The question of how the painting ended up in a thrift store has yet to be answered, but the auction house does have one theory. They suspect that book publisher Little, Brown and Company had offered the "Ramona" painting as a gift. It might have been given to either a book editor or to the book author's estate.

Leland said that discoveries such as this are rare. Thrift-store hounds shouldn't get their hopes up that they will find similar lost paintings. "It is difficult for anyone other than an expert in antiques or fine art to be able to recognize the significance of what they have found."

title: NASA's OSIRIS-REx probe successfully delivers asteroid Bennu samples to Earth
zhTitle: 贝努小行星的样本回到地球
reason: 七年任务、四十亿英里，以及着陆点中途更改的原因。

cover.caption: NASA's OSIRIS-REx returned to Earth in September, dropping off NASA's first-ever asteroid sample in the Utah desert, where it was rushed away to a secure facility to be opened and then studied.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: NASA's OSIRIS-REx probe successfully delivers asteroid Bennu samples to Earth
levels.body:
NASA collected samples from an asteroid. NASA is the U.S. space agency. An asteroid is a small rocky object. Asteroids orbit the sun like planets do, though asteroids are much smaller.

Those samples finally landed on Earth. The space capsule landed on September 24. Teams from NASA and the U.S. Air Force collected the capsule. It landed in the Utah desert.

This is the first time NASA has taken an asteroid sample. And it is the first time NASA got the sample back from space.

The Mission

The asteroid is called Bennu. The mission took seven years to complete.

OSIRIS-REx is the spacecraft that collected the samples. It launched from Earth in 2016. The spacecraft arrived at Bennu in 2018. There, scientists learned the asteroid looked like a pile of gravel and rubble. They thought it would look like solid rock. The scientists had to make a new plan.

OSIRIS-REx had a new landing site. It was much smaller than the first one. But the spacecraft landed. The craft collected samples in 2020. Then, OSIRIS-REx left Bennu in 2021.

The trip was more than 4 billion miles. That's about 6.2 billion kilometers. That is a long long trip to Bennu and back to Earth.

The Capsule

OSIRIS-REx did not land on Earth. It stayed above Earth. It let go of the capsule that held the samples. The capsule fell 63,000 miles. That's about 101,000 kilometers above Earth. The fall took less than 10 minutes in total.

Once on the ground, teams collected the capsule. They checked for damage. But the capsule looked whole. It was not broken. They hooked the capsule up to a helicopter. They took it to a temporary clean room.

Scientists then opened the capsule. Inside was a canister. It held the actual asteroid samples. Teams prepared the sample. They took it to Houston, Texas. That's where NASA's Johnson Space Center (JSC) is.

What Will Come Of The Samples?

NASA now has 8.8 ounces of material from Bennu. That's about 250 grams. Scientists plan to study the samples. They have many questions. They want to learn about Earth. And they want to learn about the solar system.

NASA will keep most of the sample. It will keep about 70 percent. The rest of the asteroid will be shared with other scientists. About 200 scientists will share 25 percent of the sample. The Canadian Space Agency will get 4 percent. The space agency in Japan will get the smallest amount.

figures.caption: NASA's OSIRIS-REx returned to Earth in September, dropping off NASA's first-ever asteroid sample in the Utah desert, where it was rushed away to a secure facility to be opened and then studied.
An artist's rendering shows OSIRIS-REx spacecraft descending toward asteroid Bennu to collect a sample of the asteroid's surface.
The sample return capsule from NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission is seen shortly after touching down in the desert at the Department of Defense's Utah Test and Training Range.

levels.name: 基础
levels.title: NASA's OSIRIS-REx probe successfully delivers asteroid Bennu samples to Earth
levels.body:
NASA, the U.S. space agency, has collected samples from an asteroid. Those samples finally landed on Earth. An asteroid is a small rocky object. Asteroids orbit the sun like planets do, though asteroids are much smaller.

The space capsule landed on September 24. Teams from NASA and the U.S Air Force collected the capsule. It landed in the Utah desert.

This is the first time NASA has taken and recovered a sample of an asteroid.

"Touchdown for science!" said Jim Garvin. He is a chief scientist of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. "For the first time in history, we brought goodies back home from this kind of object. This is so huge and we're all breathing a big sigh of relief."

The Mission

The asteroid is called Bennu. The mission to collect samples took seven years to complete.

OSIRIS-REx is the space craft that collected the samples. It launched from Earth in 2016. The spacecraft arrived at Bennu in 2018. There, scientists learned the asteroid was more like a pile of gravel and rubble than a solid rock. Scientists had to rethink Osiris-REx's landing. They came up with a plan. The spacecraft landed on a site less than one-quarter of the size of its original intended landing site. The craft collected samples in 2020, and then left Bennu in 2021.

The trip was over 4 billion miles (6.2 billion kilometers) to reach Bennu and back to Earth.

OSIRIS-REx released its sample capsule. The spacecraft was about 63,000 miles (101,000 kilometers) above Earth. The capsule contains some 8.8 ounces (250 grams) of material from Bennu. Scientists plan to study the samples. They want to learn about the origins of life on Earth and the early days of our solar system.

The OSIRIS-REx capsule fell through the atmosphere at speeds of up to 27,000 miles per hour (43,450 kilometers per hour). The atmosphere is the layer of gases that surrounds the planet. During the fall, the capsule got very hot. The temperature was as high as 5,300 degrees Fahrenheit (2,900 Celsius).

The Capsule

The capsule cooled as it floated down to the desert floor. The fall took under 10 minutes in total.

Once on the ground, teams made sure it was safe to approach the capsule. They also saw that the capsule wasn't broken. From there, teams hooked the capsule up to a helicopter. They took it to a temporary clean room.

Once secured inside the facility, the capsule was opened. Inside the capsule is a cannister that holds samples. Teams prepared to transport the cannister. The asteroid material will head to Houston, Texas. That's where NASA's Johnson Space Center (JSC) is.

What Will Come Of The Samples?

The space capsule with samples landed in the Utah desert. Teams with NASA and the U.S Air Force recovered the capsule.

"Touchdown for science!" said Jim Garvin, chief scientist of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. "For the first time in history, we brought goodies back home from this kind of object. This is so huge and we're all breathing a big sigh of relief."

The Mission

The successful landing and recovery of the asteroid Bennu samples marks the end of a seven-year mission.

OSIRIS-REx, the space craft that collected the samples, launched from Earth in 2016. The spacecraft arrived at Bennu in 2018. There, it found an asteroid resembling more of a pile of gravel and rubble than a solid rock. Scientists with the mission then had to rethink the plan for the probe's landing. Instead, the spacecraft had to land in an area less than one-quarter of the size of its original intended landing site. The craft collected samples in 2020, and then left Bennu in 2021.

The entire trip was over 4 billion miles (6.2 billion kilometers) to reach Bennu and then make the journey home.

The capsule contains some 8.8 ounces (250 grams) of rocks and other material from Bennu. These materials could help answer some of scientists' most burning questions about the origins of life on Earth and the early days of our solar system.

The capsule deployed its main parachute at an altitude of about 20,000 feet (6,100 meters). This was four times higher than expected at 5,000 feet (1,500 meters). The capsule appeared to land safely.

As the sample return capsule floated down to the desert floor, the capsule cooled down enough so that U.S. Air Force personnel could approach after locating it. The descent from the edge of the atmosphere to the desert sands took under 10 minutes in total.

"Congratulations to the entire OSIRIS-REx team. You did it!" NASA Administrator Bill Nelson said in a video during live commentary. "This mission proves that NASA does big things. Things that inspire us, things that unite us, things that show that nothing is beyond our reach."
