levels.body:
DUGWAY PROVING GROUND, Utah — NASA's first-ever samples of an asteroid in deep space have landed safely on Earth in a historic first for the United States.

In a midmorning operation at the U.S. Army's Dugway Proving Ground in the arid Utah desert, teams with NASA and the U.S. Air Force successfully recovered a space capsule with samples of asteroid Bennu taken by the agency's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft in 2020. The mission marks the first time that NASA has taken a sample of an asteroid, not to mention successfully recovering it.

After traveling for over 4 billion miles (6.2 billion kilometers) to reach Bennu and then make the journey home, the OSIRIS-REx probe released its sample return capsule on September 24, while it was about 63,000 miles (101,000 kilometers) above Earth. The capsule contains some 250 grams (8.8 ounces) of rocks and other material from Bennu, material that could help answer some of scientists' most burning questions about the origins of life on Earth and the early days of our solar system.

"Touchdown for science!" Jim Garvin, chief scientist of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, said from the landing site during a live broadcast. "For the first time in history, we brought goodies back home from this kind of object. This is so huge and we're all breathing a big sigh of relief."

The OSIRIS-REx capsule reached speeds of up to 27,000 miles per hour (43,450 kilometers per hour) and its heatshield experienced temperatures as high as 5,300 degrees Fahrenheit (2,900 Celsius) as it descended through Earth's atmosphere.

The capsule deployed its main parachute at an altitude of about 20,000 feet, four times higher than expected at 5,000 feet, but it appeared to land safely. Officials with NASA and Lockheed Martin Space Systems, which built OSIRIS-REx, told reporters in the post-landing conference that the drogue chute likely deployed, but was just not seen on cameras monitoring the descent.

"The bottom line is we landed. When the main parachute came out, that was the moment I was waiting for," Mike Moreau, OSIRIS-REx recovery team lead at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, said in the briefing. "The drogue's on top of the main parachute, so it all had to come out," he added.

As the sample return capsule floated down to the desert floor of the U.S. Department of Defense's Utah Test and Training Range, the capsule cooled down enough so that U.S. Air Force personnel could approach after locating it.

The descent from the edge of the atmosphere to the desert sands took under 10 minutes in total to end a 4 billion-mile journey. The $1 billion OSIRIS-REx mission launched in 2016, arrived at Bennu in 2018 and collected samples of the asteroid in 2020.

"Boy, did we stick the landing," Dante Lauretta, principal investigator of the OSIRIS-REx mission, said in a post-landing briefing.

Once on the ground, the capsule and surrounding area was examined to make sure it was safe for OSIRIS-REx team members and recovery personnel to approach and examine the capsule. An early examination by recovery teams found that the capsule was intact and suffered no breaches during landing.

From there, the capsule was hooked up to a helicopter via a longline and airlifted to a temporary cleanroom set up at the U.S. Army's Dugway Proving Ground.

Once secured inside the facility, the capsule was opened, and the canister inside that contains the precious sample of asteroid Bennu will be prepared for transport once again. The asteroid material will next be loaded onto an aircraft and flown to NASA's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston, Texas, where a newly built facility is waiting for it, the agency's Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science (ARES) division.

"Congratulations to the entire OSIRIS-REx team. You did it!" NASA Administrator Bill Nelson said in a video during live commentary. "This mission proves that NASA does big things. Things that inspire us, things that unite us, things that show that nothing is beyond our reach."

From there, the sample will be divided among different scientific institutions and world space agencies. NASA will keep 70 percent of the sample at JSC where it will analyze it for years to come. Twenty-five percent will be shared between over 200 scientists at 35 different facilities. Four percent will be given to the Canadian Space Agency, and 0.5 percent will be given to the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).

OSIRIS-REx is NASA's first to collect an asteroid sample, but JAXA has two such missions under its belt. That agency's Hayabusa 1 collected materials from asteroid Itokawa and returned them in 2010, and Hayabusa 2 returned samples from asteroid Ryugu in 2020.

The successful landing and recovery of the asteroid Bennu samples marks the end of a seven-year mission that saw its share of surprises. When the spacecraft arrived at Bennu in 2018, it found an asteroid resembling more of a pile of gravel and rubble than a solid rock. Scientists with the mission then had to rethink the plan for the probe's landing, which required reprogramming the spacecraft to land in an area less than one-quarter of the size of its original intended landing site.

But the OSIRIS-REx team pulled it off. Lauretta said during a pre-landing media briefing on September 22 that the OSIRIS-REx team has been consistent in its ability to work through the unexpected issues that popped up.

"We've always taken a deliberate, careful, cautious approach," Lauretta said. "And I think that's why this mission has been so successful up to this date."

title: Shell hunters find treasures that Hurricane Lee left on North Carolina's beaches

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Shell hunters find treasures that Hurricane Lee left on North Carolina's beaches
levels.body:
A hurricane caused huge waves in North Carolina in September 2023. A hurricane is a big storm. It has very high winds. It can also have rain, thunder and lightning. A hurricane can do a lot of damage. People name storms to keep track of the damage. This hurricane was called Lee.

The winds from Hurricane Lee caused big waves. Hurricane Lee brought lots of seashells onto North Carolina's beaches. That made shell hunters very happy.

Seashells are made by sea animals. Shells are a hard, outer layer. They protect the animal that lives inside. Animals such as clams have shells. So do scallops and sea snails.

North Carolina's beaches were full of whelk shells. Whelks are sea snails. They have beautiful, spiraled shells. There were also smaller shells called olives. They are made by olive sea snails. There were even hard-to-find shells like the Scotch bonnet.

What Have Shell Hunters Found?

Laura Castro is a shell collector. She saw a photo of a pickup truck. It amazed her. It was full of whelks! They were found on the Outer Banks. This is a string of islands. They are on the coast of North Carolina.

But Castro found something exciting, too. It was a lion's paw scallop shell. They are rare in North Carolina.

Experts say it is not always a good idea to take shells. It may harm the beaches. Birds use shells for their nests. Fish use shells to hide from enemies. So do small crabs. A shoreline can wear away more quickly without shells.

levels.name: 进阶
levels.title: Shell hunters find treasures that Hurricane Lee left on North Carolina's beaches
levels.body:
Hurricane Lee churned up school-bus-sized waves in North Carolina in September 2023. Hurricanes are large storms with strong winds. Those winds can cause big waves. And those big waves turned several North Carolina beaches into treasure troves for shell hunters. The beaches were full of seashells from the storm.

A seashell is a hard, protective outer layer. Seashells are made by some animals that live in the sea. Every empty shell on a beach was once part of an animal. The shells could have belonged to an animal like a clam, scallop, oyster or snail. When these animals die, their shells are left behind.

North Carolina's beaches were full of whelk shells. Whelks are sea snails. They have beautiful, spiraled shells. There were also smaller shells called olives. Olive snails make shells that are long and smooth. There were even hard-to-find shells like the Scotch bonnet. This is another type of sea snail. But as big hurricanes sometimes do, Hurricane Lee left even rarer shells.

What Have Shell Hunters Found?

The storm left large amounts of shells after it passed. In some places, collectors said, it was hard to walk on the sand or wade in the surf. They'd always be hitting a whelk or a piece of driftwood.

Shell collector Laura Castro groaned with envy over a photo. It was of a pickup truck full of whelks gathered on the Outer Banks. This is a string of islands that lie along the coast of North Carolina. The Outer Banks saw the storm's biggest waves.

Still, Castro managed to enlarge her own collection. She found an unbroken lion's paw scallop shell at Bear Island. The shells of these scallops are rarely found on North Carolina beaches. That's because the scallops live in deep, dark water. They often live more than 100 feet down. But the storm brought some shells ashore.

Some experts warn against taking seashells from the beach. They say it could hurt the environment. Seashells are an important part of the coast's ecosystem. An ecosystem is a biological community of plants, animals and tiny living things. Birds use seashells to build their nests. Seagrasses and sponges live on them. Fish and hermit crabs use shells to hide from enemies. Removing shells and shell fragments could also change how quickly a shoreline might wear away.

The Best Beaches To Find Shells

No two hurricanes are exactly alike. One storm can cover one section of beach in shells. At the same time, it can wipe miles of nearby shore clean. Still, the beaches below are recommended for shell hunting in North Carolina.

- Holden Beach is an island in Brunswick County. After Hurricane Lee, it was covered with whelks and olive shells. It also had sea biscuits. These are round-shaped animals that live in the sea. They look like puffy versions of their relative, the sand dollar. The sea biscuits were fossils, which are the remains of plants or animals preserved in rock. The sea biscuit fossils were millions of years old. The strong waves pushed the fossils out on the beach from the deep water.

- Cape Point is part of the Cape Hatteras National Seashore. A cape is a narrow piece of land. It stretches out into the ocean. Cape Point had many different types of whelks. Collectors found whale bone fossils. There were even octopi!

- Bear Island can be reached by ferry from Hammocks Beach State Park. The waves brought in shells like the lion's paw scallop that Castro found.

Hurricane season lasts through November.

- Shackleford Banks is part of the Cape Lookout National Seashore. This island is a good place to find big whelks and sand dollars.

levels.title: Shell hunters find treasures that Hurricane Lee left on North Carolina's beaches
levels.body:
Tractor-trailer-sized waves churned up by Hurricane Lee in mid-September 2023 turned several North Carolina beaches into fertile grounds for shell hunters.

The ocean spit out huge numbers of shells, including a wide variety of types of whelks, plus smaller shells such as olives and even hard-to-find Scotch bonnets, the official shell of North Carolina.

But as big hurricanes sometimes do, Hurricane Lee also deposited specimens not typically found within hundreds of miles of the North Carolina coast.

What Have Shell Hunters Found?

In some places, collectors said, it was hard to walk on the sand or wade in the surf without hitting a whelk or a piece of driftwood a day or two after the storm had passed.

"Ohhhh," Laura Castro said, groaning with envy on September 18 over a Facebook photo she saw over the weekend showing the bed of a pickup truck full of whelks gathered on the Outer Banks, which saw the biggest waves from the storm.

But Castro, who lives on Emerald Isle, managed to expand her own collection, finding an intact lion's paw scallop shell at Bear Island, part of Hammocks Beach State Park. Those are rarely found on North Carolina beaches because they live in deep, dark water, often more than 100 feet down.

Some experts warn against removing seashells because it can adversely affect the environment. Seashells are an important part of coastal ecosystems. They provide materials for birds' nests and host other marine life like algae, sea grass and sponges. Fish and hermit crabs use them to hide from predators. The removal of large shells and shell fragments could also alter how quickly a shoreline might erode.

The Best Beaches To Find Shells

While thousands of shells have been harvested by collectors, many of whom posted photos of their hauls on social media, several North Carolina beaches still may yield better-than-average buckets full for the next several days.

No two hurricanes are exactly alike, and beach excursion guide Ray Stallings of Hatteras Island says the same storm can cover one section of beach in shells while leaving miles of adjacent shoreline wiped completely clean.

- Holden Beach, a Brunswick County island where a re-nourishment project delivered tons of fossilized sea biscuits in the spring, was covered again with those, whelks and olive shells following Hurricane Lee.

- Cape Point, part of the Cape Hatteras National Seashore, which juts into the Atlantic like an Outer Banks elbow, received maybe the greatest bounty from Hurricane Lee. The beach, accessible by permitted four-wheel-drive vehicles or by a lengthy walk from Ramps 43 and 44 off of North Carolina Highway 12, had a profusion of whelks of different sizes and types. Collectors also have found fossilized whale vertebrae and driftwood along the beach, as well as a number of octopi.

- In Buxton, also on Hatteras Island, Melinda Meadows said on September 18 that guests at her Cape Hatteras Motel came in over the weekend with buckets of shells.

- Bear Island, accessible by ferry from Hammocks Beach State Park, is a popular destination for shell hunters year-round. Hurricane Lee added to the treasures there, bringing in specimens like the lion's paw scallop shell Castro found. While some of the shells were on the beach, Castro said her best finds from the storm have been partially buried in the edge of the surf.

Hurricane season lasts through November.

- Shackleford Banks, a barrier island system off Carteret County and part of the Cape Lookout National Seashore, is always a good place to find big whelks and sand dollars, but the National Park Service said on September 18 that guests returning from the Banks over the weekend were hauling buckets heavy with fresh finds. The Banks are accessible by private boat or ferry.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: What did they find in the West Point time capsule from 1829?
levels.body:
A time capsule was opened on August 28, 2023. A time capsule is a box that holds items to be found many years later. The items are important to the people who fill the box. The time capsule is often buried or hidden for years.

This box was at the United States Military Academy at West Point in New York. It is a military school. The box was filled in 1829. It was placed inside the bottom of a statue.

The statue was of Thaddeus Kosciuszko. He helped the United States during the Revolutionary War. The war lasted from 1775 to 1783.

The box was found almost 200 years after it was hidden in the statue. That was in May 2023, But what was inside?

At First, Disappointment

An event was planned to open the box. A crowd came to see what was in the time capsule. People were excited before the box was opened.

People were disappointed when the box seemed to have only dirt inside.

But later, a better search through the dirt turned up six silver coins. They were made from 1795 to 1828. A medal to celebrate the Erie Canal was also found in the dirt. The canal is a waterway that was completed in 1825. It connected the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean.

The Mystery Box

Steve Gilland is the leader of the academy. At the start, he said no one knew what was in the box. More than 5,000 people also watched the event online. He said that it would "be better than Geraldo."

He was talking about Geraldo Rivera. He is a journalist. Many people watched on TV in 1986 as Rivera opened a secret space that was owned by a famous lawbreaker. That person was Al Capone. The space was empty.

At first, the box at West Point seemed empty, too.

More Careful Searching

Paul Hudson is an archaeologist at West Point. Archaeologists study human history. They often dig up old sites. When Hudson reached into the box, he found only dust.

At the box opening event, the box did not live up to people's hopes, Hudson said.

But he was not ready to stop looking. Hudson did not think someone would put an empty box in the statue.

So he looked more carefully through the dirt.

His search afterward turned up the coins and medal.

People at the event heard more about Kosciuszko. He was a leader from Poland, a country in Europe.

Kosciuszko was known for fighting for freedom.

levels.title: What did they find in the West Point time capsule from 1829?
levels.body:
In 1829, a metal box was closed and placed into the bottom of a monument at a U.S. military academy. The monument was for Revolutionary War hero Thaddeus Kosciuszko.

The box held items from the 1820s and was meant to be opened later. Almost 200 years passed, and in May 2023, the time capsule box was found.

An event was planned to open the box. A crowd came to see what had been put into the 1829 time capsule at the United States Military Academy at West Point in New York. Excitement was building before the August 28, 2023, reveal.

Cadets at the academy had wondered on social media what might be inside. Would the box hold an American flag, boots, old maps of West Point, or maybe dining hall silverware?

The crowd left disappointed, as the opening of the box showed only silt or dirt deposits.

Coins And A Canal Medal

Later, a closer search through the dust revealed six silver coins dating from 1795 to 1828. Their values ranged from 1 cent to a dollar. An 1826 medal honoring the Erie Canal was also discovered in the dirt. The waterway was completed in 1825, connecting the Great Lakes with the Atlantic Ocean.

"Nobody has any idea what's inside of it," U.S. Military Academy leader Steve Gilland had said at the start of the ceremony, which was also seen by more than 5,000 viewers online. "You all are here and are going to see it with all of us." He also said, "It's going to be better than Geraldo."

"Geraldo" was Geraldo Rivera. In 1986, 30 million viewers watched on TV as he opened a secret space kept by famous lawbreaker Al Capone. The opened space contained only dust.

Another leader at the academy, Shane Reeves, also mentioned Rivera at the event.

Three Box Options

Reeves said there were three options for what might happen as they opened the box. The first was that they would find nothing, similar to Rivera's event.

Reeves said someone told him that if "we had a sense of humor, we would have asked Mr. Rivera to be up here with us. [Maybe] we should have done that.'"

The second option would be finding only dust, Reeves said. A third option, he said, would be to find "amazing, historic" items.

The event was a mix of the first and second possibilities.

Hiding Under The Silt And Rocks

Paul Hudson is an archaeologist at West Point. Archaeologists study human history, often by digging up sites. When Hudson reached into the box, he found only dust and silt, bits of rock and dirt.

Opening the box did not live up to everyone's hopes for it, Hudson said. "There is a layer of silt. That's what we were removing here that settled in the bottom." It appears that water got into the box, he said.

But Hudson was not ready to give up on finding something in the box.

"We don't want to think that they went to all the trouble to put this box in the monument and not put anything in it," he said. "We're going to collect all the silt at a later point. We'll screen it through a fine mesh screen to see if we can find any remains in it."

His work after the event turned up the coins and the medal.

"A Son Of Liberty"

Those who attended heard more about Kosciuszko. He was admired by George Washington and was a friend of Thomas Jefferson. Kosciuszko was a leader from Poland.

Jefferson called him "as pure a son of liberty as I have ever known," Reeves said.

Sam Watson, a professor in the academy's history department, said he thought about why Kosciuszko would get a monument.

"He wasn't an American," Watson said. "They didn't choose George Washington. They didn't choose Thomas Jefferson." People chose someone who could represent the fight for freedom around the world, he said.

Watson said Kosciuszko fought for freedom in Poland, calling him "the George Washington of his country."

"He Who Bravely Dares"

While those who came to watch walked away without the excitement of the moment they were hoping for, they left with an appreciation for history and for Kosciuszko. He was admired by George Washington and befriended by Thomas Jefferson.

Jefferson called the patriot from Poland "as pure a son of liberty as I have ever known," Reeves said.

"Kosciuszko was an international figure. He wasn't an American," Watson said. "They didn't choose George Washington. They didn't choose Thomas Jefferson." People chose someone who could represent the connections the American Revolution had to the fight for freedom around the world, he said.

Watson said Kosciuszko fought for freedom in Poland, calling him "the George Washington of his country."

The ceremony's last word was left to Charles Petigru, from the West Point Class of 1829, who had written a speech about Kosciuszko. Reading it at the ceremony was Devon Smith, a history major from the class of 2024.

"Let us learn from him that glory in great and honorable undertakings is not dependent upon success," Smith read. "That he who bravely dares for the good of his country … is always sure of his reward and of people's gratitude."

levels.body:

Lee was a United States Military Academy cadet at West Point in New York. But, in the end, while there was mention of General Washington, the event resulted in general disappointment.

"You all are here and are going to see it with all of us. I guarantee you it's going to be better than Geraldo."

"Geraldo" was Geraldo Rivera, who had drawn 30 million viewers to watch him "open" Al Capone's secret Chicago, Illinois, vault on live TV in 1986, only to "reveal" dust and debris.

There were three options for the morning's reveal, Reeves said. The first option was that it could be nothing, akin to Rivera's event.

"I was told yesterday that if we had a sense of humor, we would have asked Mr. Rivera to be up here with us," Reeves said. "I was like, 'We should have done that.'"

Option 2, Reeves said, would be reaching a hand into the box only to find dust, "very much like Indiana Jones in 'Raiders of the Lost Ark,' except we don't want the Angel of Death to come out and melt our faces off, so we're going to hope for not that."

There was a third option, he said: "There are amazing, historic artifacts, something we didn't even know or think about."

They should have booked Geraldo Rivera for what turned out to be a mix of the first and second possibilities.

Unmet Expectations

When Paul Hudson, the West Point archaeologist, reached his gloved hand into the unsealed lead box, he retrieved only dust and crumbling bits of dirt the color of pale ash.

"The box didn't quite meet expectations," Hudson said. "There is a layer of silt. That's what we were removing here that settled in the bottom. The bottom had bowed out. It appears to have been from moisture penetration."

"We don't want to think that they went to all the trouble to put this box in the monument and not put anything in it," he said. "We're going to collect all the silt at a later point. We'll screen it through a fine mesh screen to see if we can find any remains in it and determine what, if anything, was in here. Potentially, it was something small and organic that may have come apart over time, but we're just not certain."

It was Jefferson, Reeves said, who called the Polish patriot "as pure a son of liberty as I have ever known."

"Kosciuszko was an international figure. He wasn't an American," Watson said. "They didn't choose George Washington. They didn't choose Thomas Jefferson. They didn't choose one of the Adamses, someone obvious from the generation of Founding Fathers. They chose someone who could embody the connections the American Revolution had to revolution, to democracy, to the fight for freedom around the world."

"Kosciuszko had fought for freedom against the Russians occupying Poland. He really was not just an engineer, not just a military leader, not just a revolutionary. He's all of those things," Watson said. "He was really the George Washington of his country."

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Ancient Indigenous earthworks in Ohio named UNESCO World Heritage sites
levels.body:
A group of old mounds in Ohio is now a World Heritage site. It is the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks. It is protected by a group called UNESCO. The group's name is short for United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. It chooses the sites. They are picked because they are important to culture, history and science.

Many people want to keep the site safe. They include Ohio History Connection and Indigenous tribes. They worked together to make sure the earthworks were recognized. They said the mounds are special.

The earthworks are made up of eight sites. They are in southern Ohio. One is on a golf course. The Hopewell sites are now even more important. Other World Heritage sites include Machu Picchu in Peru and the Great Wall of China.

Skills On Display

Chief Glenna Wallace is from the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma. She is very excited about the World Heritage designation.

Wallace said everyone should see the skills of the earthwork builders. She said her ancestors were smart and talented.

The earthworks were made thousands of years ago near the Ohio River. People traveled to them from far away. Archaeologists found things from distant places. Some were from the Rocky Mountains in Colorado.

Recognizing America's Indigenous People

Deb Haaland works for the United States government. She said UNESCO recognizes America's Indigenous people.

Audrey Azoulay is with UNESCO. She said the site is an important part of American history. It is one of the biggest earthwork structures in the world.

It Took Many People And Years

The National Congress of American Indians supported the UNESCO listing. So did the Seneca Nation of New York State. The Inter-Tribal Council represents tribes in Northeast Oklahoma. It backed it, too.

Megan Wood is in charge of Ohio History Connection. She said it took more than ten years to add the site. Tribes and the National Park Service helped.

There are five sites in Chillicothe, Ohio. They are Mound City Group, Hopewell Mound Group, Seip Earthworks, High Bank Earthworks and Hopeton Earthworks. They are part of Hopewell Culture National Historical Park.

Fort Ancient Earthworks and Great Circle Earthworks are two more sites. Octagon Earthworks is the last. It is on a golf course.

Ohio Governor Mike DeWine thinks the state's first World Heritage site will bring more visitors. People will see a special part of history.

levels.name: 基础
levels.title: Ancient Indigenous earthworks in Ohio named UNESCO World Heritage sites
levels.body:
A group of ancient Indigenous ceremonial and burial mounds in Ohio was added to the list of UNESCO World Heritage sites on September 19, 2023. UNESCO is short for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. A World Heritage site has cultural, historical, scientific or other importance. It is legally protected through UNESCO.

Groups of people want to protect the sites. They include Ohio History Connection and Indigenous tribes with ties to the area. They worked together to get the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks recognized. They said that the earthworks are in good shape and are culturally important. They called them "masterpieces of human genius."

The earthworks are made up of eight sites. They are located across 90 miles (150 kilometers) in southern Ohio. This includes a mound on a private golf course and country club. The designation puts the Hopewell sites in the same group as famous places like Machu Picchu and the Great Wall of China.

Feeling Excited And Thoughtful

Chief Glenna Wallace is from the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma. She said that she felt very excited about the World Heritage designation.

Wallace said, "Tears came to my eyes, and exhilaration turned into reflection." She added that it is important for the world to see and recognize the spirituality, artistic skills and architectural knowledge of their ancestors who created the earthworks. She described her ancestors as true geniuses.

The earthworks were built between 2,000 and 1,600 years ago near the Ohio River. People from different parts of the continent came to these sites for ceremonies. Archaeologists found things from as far away as the Rocky Mountains. The Rocky Mountains are in Colorado.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Everything you need to know about North America's "ring of fire" eclipse
levels.body:
Something rare is happening in the sky soon: a solar eclipse. This happens when the moon passes between the sun and Earth. The eclipse is happening on October 14.

Sometimes during an eclipse, the moon completely blocks the sun. That is a total eclipse.

The eclipse on October 14 will not be a total eclipse. It will be an annular solar eclipse. The moon will not completely cover the sun. It will make a "ring of fire."

What Is An Annular Solar Eclipse?

The moon is not always the same distance from us. The moon orbits around the Earth. An orbit is a regular, repeating path. The moon has an elliptical orbit. This means it is shaped like an oval.

Sometimes, the moon is at its farthest distance from Earth. This makes the moon appear smaller. At other times, the moon is at its closest distance to Earth. This makes the moon appear larger.

The October 14 eclipse will be visible in North America. It will also be visible in Central and South America. Not everyone will see a ring of fire, though. Most will see a partial solar eclipse. The sun, moon and Earth will not line up perfectly. Only part of the sun will disappear. It will look like a crescent.

Some people will be able to see the annular solar eclipse. This means that they will see the ring of fire. It will only be visible in a certain path. This path is 118 to 137 miles wide. That is 190 to 220 kilometers wide. It will stretch from Oregon through California. The path will also cover parts of Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Texas. It will then move over Mexico. Next, it will move over parts of Central America and South America.

Where To See The Partial Solar Eclipse

Most people in the Americas will not see a ring of fire. They will experience a partial solar eclipse. This means they will see the sun as a crescent shape. Here is how much of the sun will be covered in the 10 biggest cities. It also includes the times when you can see the partial eclipse.

- New York, New York: 23 percent at 1:22 p.m. EDT

- Los Angeles, California: 71 percent at 9:24 a.m. PDT

- Chicago, Illinois: 43 percent at 11:58 a.m. CDT

- Houston, Texas: 85 percent at 11:58 a.m. CDT

- Phoenix, Arizona: 79 percent at 9:31 a.m. MST

- Philadelphia, Pennsylvania: 25 percent at 1:21 p.m. EDT

- San Antonio, Texas: ring of fire at 11:52 a.m. CDT

- San Diego, California: 68 percent at 9:26 a.m. PDT

- Dallas, Texas: 80 percent at 11:52 a.m. CDT

- San Jose, California: 75 percent at 9:20 a.m. PDT

How To Safely View The Partial And Annular Solar Eclipse

The sun can burn your eyes. This is still true during an eclipse. Wear solar eclipse glasses. They will protect you. Be careful with cameras, telescopes and binoculars. They need special lens filters.

From left to right, a total solar eclipse, annular solar eclipse, and partial solar eclipse. A hybrid eclipse appears as either a total or an annular eclipse (the left and middle images), depending on the observer's location.

A solar eclipse is coming soon. On October 14, people in North America will be able to view it. A solar eclipse happens when, at just the right moment, the moon passes between the sun and Earth. During a total solar eclipse, the moon completely blocks the sun's light.

The eclipse on October 14 will not be a total eclipse. It will be something called an annular solar eclipse. This happens when the moon does not completely cover the sun. So it makes a thin outer "ring of fire."

What Is An Annular Solar Eclipse?

This eclipse won't darken skies. That's because it won't fully cover the disk of the sun.

Whether the moon can completely cover the sun depends on the moon's distance from Earth. The moon has a slightly elliptical orbit around Earth. An orbit is a regular, repeating path that one object in space takes around another one. An elliptical orbit is shaped like an oval.

This means that at one point during each month, the moon is at its farthest distance from Earth. This makes it appear slightly smaller than usual. At another point each month, the moon is at its closest distance to Earth. This makes it appear slightly larger than usual.

On October 14, all of North America and Central America will experience a partial solar eclipse. Most of South America will experience one, too. A partial solar eclipse happens when the moon passes between the sun and Earth. But the sun, moon and Earth are not perfectly lined up. Only part of the sun will appear to be covered. This gives it a crescent shape.

The annular solar eclipse, or ring of fire, will not be visible everywhere. It will only be visible in a certain path. This path is 118 to 137 miles wide. That is 190 to 220 kilometers wide. It will stretch from Oregon through California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Texas. It will then move across the Gulf of Mexico and over Mexico. Next, it will move over parts of Central America and South America.

Where To See The Partial Solar Eclipse

On October 14, everyone in the United States will experience a partial solar eclipse. This means that people will see the sun in a crescent shape. Here is how much of the sun will be covered in the 10 biggest cities. It also includes the times when you can see the partial eclipse.

- New York, New York: 23 percent at 1:22 p.m. EDT

- Los Angeles, California: 71 percent at 9:24 a.m. PDT

The eclipse on October 14 will not be a total solar eclipse. It will be something called an annular solar eclipse. This happens when the moon does not completely cover the sun and makes an outer "ring of fire."

What Is An Annular Solar Eclipse?

This eclipse won't darken skies as the total solar eclipse of 2017 did. That's because it won't fully cover the disk of the sun.

This means that at one point during each month, the moon is at its farthest distance from Earth. This makes it appear slightly smaller than usual. At another point each month, the moon is at its closest distance to Earth. This makes it appear slightly larger than usual.

On October 14, all of North America and Central America and most of South America will experience a solar eclipse. For all of that region, the spectacle will be a partial solar eclipse. A partial solar eclipse happens when the moon passes between the sun and Earth but the sun, moon and Earth are not perfectly lined up. Only part of the sun will appear to be covered, giving it a crescent shape.

Only within a small range will the annular solar eclipse, or the ring of fire, be visible. In fact, the path where you can see the ring of fire is only 118 to 137 miles (190 to 220 kilometers) wide. That path will stretch from Oregon through Northern California, northeast Nevada, central Utah, northeast Arizona, southwest Colorado, central New Mexico and southern Texas. It will then move across the Gulf of Mexico and over Mexico, as well as parts of Central America and South America.

Viewers in Nicaragua and Costa Rica will be able to view the ring of fire longest. They could see a ring of fire lasting 5 minutes, 17 seconds.

People at the center of the path of the moon's shadow will experience the longest eclipse. But at the northern edge of the path, you may experience a more dramatic spectacle. This includes places such as Dolores, Colorado, and Santa Fe, New Mexico.

Viewers there will see a ring of fire for just a few seconds. But it will be less circular, and one part of the edge of the moon will appear to almost block out the sun.

On October 14, most of the Americas will experience a partial solar eclipse. This means that people will see the sun in a crescent shape. Here is what the 10 biggest cities in the U.S. will experience that day, in terms of how much of the sun will be covered:

The next annular solar eclipse will occur in October 2024. A ring of fire will be visible from the Pacific Ocean, southern Chile and southern Argentina. Only a part of the sun will appear to be covered, giving it a crescent shape.

The annual solar eclipse, or ring of fire, will only be visible in some areas. In fact, the path where you can see the ring of fire is only 118 to 137 miles (190 to 220 kilometers) wide. That path will stretch from Oregon through Northern California, northeast Nevada, central Utah, northeast Arizona, southwest Colorado, central New Mexico and southern Texas. It will then move across the Gulf of Mexico and over Mexico, as well as parts of Central America and South America.

Viewers in Nicaragua and Costa Rica will be able to view the ring of fire longest. They could see a ring of fire lasting 5 minutes, 17 seconds.

Why Will The 2023 Annular Solar Eclipse Be So Special?

It's important to be in the center of the path of the moon's shadow if you want to experience a long spectacle. However, experienced eclipse chasers will head to the northern edge of the path — at locations such as Dolores, Colorado, and Santa Fe, New Mexico — to experience a much shorter, but arguably more dramatic, spectacle.

Viewers in these locations will see a ring of fire for perhaps just a few seconds, but it will be less circular, and one part of the edge of the moon will appear to almost block out the sun.

Where To See The Partial Solar Eclipse

On October 14, most of the Americas will experience a big partial solar eclipse. This means that people will see the sun in a crescent shape. Here is what the 10 biggest cities in the U.S. will experience that day, in terms of how much of the sun will be covered by the moon:

- New York, New York: 23 percent at 1:22 p.m. EDT

- Los Angeles, California: 71 percent at 9:24 a.m. PDT

- Chicago, Illinois: 43 percent at 11:58 a.m. CDT

- Houston, Texas: 85 percent at 11:58 a.m. CDT

- Phoenix, Arizona: 79 percent at 9:31 a.m. MST

- Philadelphia, Pennsylvania: 25 percent at 1:21 p.m. EDT

- San Antonio, Texas: ring of fire at 11:52 a.m. CDT

- San Diego, California: 68 percent at 9:26 a.m.PDT

- Dallas, Texas: 80 percent at 11:52 a.m. CDT

- San Jose, California: 75 percent at 9:20 a.m. PDT

How To Safely View The Partial And Annular Solar Eclipse

Whether your location will experience a partial solar eclipse or an annular solar eclipse, the dangers are the same. Even if you can't see much sunlight, it can still burn your eyes, so observers need to wear solar eclipse glasses. Cameras, telescopes and binoculars must have solar filters placed in front of their lenses at all times.

When Is The Next Annular Solar Eclipse Ring Of Fire?

The next annular solar eclipse will occur in October 2024. A ring of fire will be visible from the Pacific Ocean, southern Chile and southern Argentina. At the point of greatest eclipse in the ocean, the ring of fire will last 7 minutes and 25 seconds, but the best spot will be Easter Island (Rapa Nui), located off the western coast of Chile. There, it will be possible to stand among the remote volcanic island's many carved statues and see a ring of fire for up to 6 minutes and 9 seconds.

On October 14, 2023, an annular solar eclipse will come to North America.

Roughly 11 years after the same type of solar eclipse crossed the U.S. Southwest on May 20, 2012, this one will be visible from a similar region, crossing eight U.S. states from Oregon to Texas, according to NASA.

During an annular solar eclipse, the moon appears slightly smaller than the sun, so it can't block the entire disk. The result is a beautiful "ring of fire." Here's everything you need to know about this rare event.

What Is An Annular Solar Eclipse?

This eclipse won't darken skies the way the total solar eclipse of August 21, 2017, did. A solar eclipse occurs when a new moon is positioned precisely between Earth and the sun and casts its shadow on Earth.

An annular solar eclipse happens when the moon appears relatively small in the sky so it does not fully cover the disk of the sun, leaving a thin outer ring often called a "ring of fire."

Whether the moon can completely cover the sun's disk depends on the moon's distance from Earth. The moon has a slightly elliptical orbit around Earth, so at two points each month, it is farthest from (apogee) and closest to (perigee) Earth, making the moon appear slightly smaller and slightly larger than average in our sky.

On October 14, 2023, the new moon will look relatively small and, therefore, cover only 91 percent of the sun's disk as viewed from the narrow path of annularity that stretches from Oregon through Texas and beyond.

On October 14, 2023, all of North America and Central America, and most of South America will experience a solar eclipse. For all of that region, the spectacle will be a partial solar eclipse of varying obscuration. Only within the path of annularity, which is 118 to 137 miles (190 to 220 kilometers) wide, will the ring of fire be visible. That path will stretch from Oregon through Northern California, northeast Nevada, central Utah, northeast Arizona, southwest Colorado, central New Mexico and southern Texas. It will then move across the Gulf of Mexico and over Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia and Brazil.

The point of greatest eclipse — where viewers could see a ring of fire lasting 5 minutes, 17 seconds — will occur off the coast of Nicaragua and Costa Rica.

The most scenic places to see the ring of fire are in the U.S. Southwest and at the Mayan temple at Edzná on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.

Why Will The 2023 Annular Solar Eclipse Be So Special?

Although it's largely being seen as a warm-up for the 2024 total solar eclipse, the 2023 annular solar eclipse is a great excuse to travel. For eclipse chasers who have yet to see an annular solar eclipse, it's a great opportunity.

As with all eclipses, it's important to be in the center of the path of the moon's shadow if you want to experience as long a spectacle as possible. That means putting yourself on or near the centerline. However, experienced eclipse chasers will head to the northern edge of the path — at locations such as Dolores, Colorado, and Santa Fe, New Mexico — to experience a much shorter, but arguably more dramatic, spectacle.

Viewers in these locations will see a ring of fire for perhaps just a few seconds. But it will be less circular, and one part of the edge of the moon will appear to almost block out the sun. This may make it possible to glimpse the "Baily's beads" ring around the moon during the annularity phase, just as can be seen during a total solar eclipse.

Where To See The Partial Solar Eclipse

Although the ring of fire will get a lot of attention, few people make much effort to travel to see an annular solar eclipse. After all, these events don't quite compare to total solar eclipses. On October 14, 2023, most of the Americas will experience a big partial solar eclipse. Here is what the 10 biggest cities in the U.S. will experience that day; only one will see the ring of fire:

- New York, New York: 23 percent at 1:22 p.m. EDT

- Los Angeles, California: 71 percent at 9:24 a.m. PDT

- Chicago, Illinois: 43 percent at 11:58 a.m. CDT

- Houston, Texas: 85 percent at 11:58 a.m. CDT

- Dallas, Texas: 80 percent at 11:52 a.m. CDT

- San Jose, California: 75 percent at 9:20 a.m. PDT

How To Safely View The Partial And Annular Solar Eclipse

To safely view this event, you must use solar filters at all times. Whether your location will experience a partial solar eclipse or an annular solar eclipse, the dangers are the same. In fact, a ring of fire is technically nothing more than a particularly pretty partial solar eclipse. At no point will more than 91 percent of the sun's disk be covered by the new moon. Observers will need to wear solar eclipse glasses, and cameras, telescopes and binoculars must have solar filters placed in front of their lenses at all times.

When Is The Next Annular Solar Eclipse Ring Of Fire?

After the annular solar eclipse on October 14, 2023, the next annular solar eclipse will occur on October 2, 2024, when a ring of fire will be visible from the Pacific Ocean, southern Chile and southern Argentina. At the point of greatest eclipse in the ocean, the ring of fire will last 7 minutes and 25 seconds, but the best spot will be Easter Island (Rapa Nui), located about 2,000 miles (3,200 kilometers) off the western coast of Chile. There, it will be possible to stand among the remote volcanic island's many carved moai statues and see a ring of fire for up to 6 minutes and 9 seconds.

title: Scientist deliberately subjects himself to the world's most painful stingers

cover.caption: Tarantula hawk wasps have one of the most painful stings. In the name of science, a scientist allowed himself to be stung by insects.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Scientist deliberately subjects himself to the world's most painful stingers
levels.body:
Insect stings can really hurt. Most people try to avoid them.

But Sam Robinson gets stung on purpose. He is a molecular biologist. Molecular biology is a branch of biology. It is the study of the molecules that make up living things.

Robinson wants to understand pain. He wants to find the chemicals that cause it. A chemical is a substance. It has a defined composition and properties used to identify it. Chemicals can occur naturally. They can also be made in a lab.

"I'm genuinely interested," he says. "I wonder, 'What does that sting feel like?' and there's often no information on that."

Research May Lead To New Drugs

Robinson rates each sting. He uses a pain scale developed by Justin Schmidt. Schmidt is an entomologist. Entomologists are scientists who study insects.

Schmidt did not get stung on purpose. But he could not avoid it.

"He worked with these insects for 40 years," says Robinson. "There's no way around it!"

Robinson writes down the intensity of the pain. He writes down how long it lasts. He describes the pain. He notes other symptoms like inflammation. Inflammation is the immune system's response to an irritant. Irritants could include a stinger.

Robinson hopes his research is helpful to other scientists. He hopes it can help them find new pain medications.

First, Robinson must figure out what makes a sting painful. He has to find the neurons that sense the pain. A neuron is a type of cell. It sends and receives messages from the body to the brain and back. Then, scientists can develop drugs that target those neurons.

New medications may be a while off. But Robinson has already had scientific breakthroughs.

In May, Robinson and his team revealed that ants produce neurotoxins. Neurotoxins are poisonous substances. They act on the victim's nervous system. They disrupt the normal function of neurons.

Most Painful Stings

Schmidt rated the bullet ant as having the most painful sting. Robinson agrees. Bullet ants live in Central and South America.

"Apparently it feels like being shot," says Robinson. That is where its name comes from. "Its bite is a really unique pain," he says. It can last for 12 hours.

Robinson says all the stings are worth it. He says people are scared of stings. But most of the time, they do not injure you. They just hurt.

"These things, they're not going to kill you," he says. And the pain eventually goes away.

figures.caption: Tarantula hawk wasps have one of the most painful stings. In the name of science, a scientist allowed himself to be stung by insects.
Some insects can extend and retract their stingers.
After a sting, toxins in the venom cause our bodies to react with pain and swelling.
The Schmidt pain index has a scale of 1 to 4. Coming in at 4, the tarantula hawk wasp and the bullet ant have one of the most painful stings.

levels.body:
Meet the man putting his body on the line — all in the name of science.

"I'm interested in what the chemicals are behind pain and how they interact with our bodies to create that pain," Sam Robinson explains to me in a casual, nonchalant tone.

But there's nothing nonchalant about the way Robinson explores his interest.

A molecular biologist at the University of Queensland's Institute for Molecular Bioscience, he has earned himself quite a reputation for his unconventional research methods, namely, for being stung by the world's most painful insects and plants, on purpose.

"I'm genuinely interested," he tells me. "I find something and I wonder 'what does that sting feel like?' and there's often no information on that, or no good quality information."

Robinson rates each sting using a pain scale developed by the late American entomologist Justin Schmidt, who was famous for his studies of stinging insects.

While Schmidt's stings weren't intentional, they were inevitable in his line of work.

"He worked with these insects for 40 years," says Robinson. "So if you're working with them for that amount of time, you get stung, there's no way around it!

"He was the first one to start recording the different experiences and he made this key observation early on that not all stings are equal. So he developed this pain scale called the Schmidt Sting Pain Index."

While the science behind each sting is complex, Robinson's methods for recording his (painful) experiences are a humble notebook and stopwatch.

"Obviously I'm writing down the intensity of the pain and how long it lasts, but also the type of pain and other symptoms, like inflammation."

Not only is Robinson documenting the effects of different stings on the human body for scientific record, but his observations have the potential to lead to significant biomedical applications.

"One of the cool things it can do is by finding new things and new targets in our own bodies, in terms of our pain-sensing neurons, we can potentially develop a new class of drugs to target that," Robinson says.

"If you can understand, at a molecular level, why something stings when it hurts, then you can potentially come up with a more rational treatment for that.

"A new class of painkillers would be the ultimate health outcome."

But while new medications may be a while off, Robinson and his colleagues have already had myriad scientific breakthroughs.

"The progress has been unbelievable actually. We've had some really amazing outcomes over the last five years or so."

In May 2023, Robinson and his team published a paper in Nature Communications, revealing for the first time that ants inflict pain with neurotoxins.

"I looked into the venom of green ants, along with a bunch of other ants, and found that this particular class of toxin was responsible for the pain," explains Robinson. "And this toxin class was new to science.

"So, for one, we didn't know that's how ants were causing this type of pain, and then, also, no one knew this class of toxin existed!

"We figured out what the toxins target in our nerves and that information is very, very useful to understand how this works at a molecular level and how it's involved in pain."

Another massive breakthrough, published in Nature Communications in 2020, was a discovery about the gympie-gympie (Dendrocnide moroides) plant: What scientists had long thought caused its excruciating sting was incorrect.

"For a long time, people thought that the long-lasting pain was because of the little spines from the leaves or stems stuck in the body — like fibreglass. But we now know that that's not the case because we've figured out what the toxin is in those stinging trees, and how it causes pain," says Robinson.

A common remedy for the infamous gympie-gympie sting is to use sticky tape or wax to remove the tiny stinging hairs from the skin.

"We now know that's completely futile because it's the toxin that's causing this long-lasting pain, it has an irreversible effect on your nerves," Robinson explains.

"It targets something in our nerves that we didn't know was involved in pain and now we know this particular protein is intricately involved in a certain type of pain.

"So that's just two examples of new things we've learned."

Most Painful Stings

The late Justin Schmidt rated the bullet ant (Paraponera clavata) — found in Central and South America — as having the most painful insect sting in the world. Robinson agrees.

"It's called a bullet ant because apparently it feels like being shot," says Robinson. "Now, I don't know what being shot feels like, but its bite is a really unique pain, a very deep, drilling, long-lasting pain. It can last for 12 hours, it's quite amazing.

"It's the most intense pain I've felt from a sting and the length of it just wears you down so that's what gives it this really high rating."

Luckily, we don't have bullet ants in Australia, but Robinson says our green ants (Rhytidoponera metallica) give the bullet ants a run for their money.

"It's a unique sort of pain, that can gradually build and then last quite a long time. It can be quite intense and quite deep."

Also high on Robinson's list of most painful stings is one from, what he calls, the "humungous" tarantula hawk wasp (Pepsis sp.).

"They are just monsters, they can be a couple of inches long, quite frightening, and they have no natural enemies — I think that's because everything knows that when they sting, it just hurts so much!

"When you're stung it's five to 10 minutes of intense pain and swelling."

Like the bullet ant, the tarantula hawk wasp is not found in Australia, but, again, we have an equivalent: the spider-hunting wasp (Heterodontonyx bicolor).

"This sting is right up there with the tarantula hawk wasp," says Robinson.

Chatting to Robinson as he relives these horrid encounters, there's one question I just have to ask: "Is it worth it?"

"Yeah," he says without hesitation.

"These things, they're not going to kill you. People are really worried about stinging things but the reality is, that for 99.9 percent of us, they're just going to cause a bit of transient pain. They're not going to do you any harm beyond that."

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: "Gentle parenting" squirrels: Millions watch TikToker care for animals on his balcony
levels.body:
Derrick Downey Jr. was relaxing at home in Los Angeles, California. A fox squirrel appeared on his balcony. They stared at each other curiously. Downey then offered the squirrel food. He found some peanuts inside his house. He returned to the balcony and offered the peanuts to the squirrel. Surprisingly, he said the squirrel pulled his hand closer and started eating.

Downey was pleased by this moment. He had been feeling low. The squirrel began visiting him every day. It often brought another squirrel along. Downey named the pair Richard and Maxine.

He posted a video on TikTok. The video showed him with the squirrels. He gave them water and asked them not to fight. His video racked up more than 26 million views. He talks to the squirrels about their feelings.

levels.title: "Gentle parenting" squirrels: Millions watch TikToker care for animals on his balcony
levels.body:
Derrick Downey Jr. was relaxing on his second-story balcony in Los Angeles, California, when a bushy-tailed fox squirrel suddenly appeared.

Downey said they stared at each other for a few seconds, and then he asked the squirrel: "Do you want something to eat?"

"It seemed obvious to me that he did, so I told him, 'Stay here, I'll be right back,'" Downey recalled.

Downey ran into his kitchen and searched in his cupboards until he'd found some peanuts, then he hurried back to the balcony.

"The squirrel was still sitting in the same spot, so I figured, 'OK, he was listening to me,'" he said. "And when I held my hand out with the peanuts, he pulled my hand closer and started eating."

Downey, who had been feeling low, was enchanted by the encounter.

"I was having a rough time, not because of the pandemic, but because of some mental health issues," Downey said.

Since that day in 2020, the squirrel has continued to scamper up to his balcony for treats, often bringing a friend with him, Downey said. He named the affable pair Richard and Maxine for no particular reason other than he liked the sound of it.

He decided to share a video on TikTok of him interacting with the squirrels. The short clip of him giving Richard and Maxine sips of water from a glass and tenderly telling them not to quarrel has racked up more than 26 million views since it was posted last year.

"Don't be fighting! Do you want some water? Come here. I know it's hot — we get agitated, we get aggravated," Downey tells the squirrels in the clip.

"You're having a moment — it's OK to have that moment," he said.

As he bonded with the squirrels, he started to feel better himself.

"Going outside and connecting with nature was my gateway to relief from depression," he said. "It brought me peace. I would see Richard walking around, and talking to him made me feel good about the world."

His TikTok and Instagram followers loved the videos of him getting to know the squirrels and talking to them.

"Validate their moments and emotions. You're the best squirrel dad!" someone commented.

Downey replied: "Mental health is important. Gotta make sure they're good mentally and physically."

Another person commented, "He's gentle parenting the squirrels." And another said, "Bro treats squirrels better than my parents treat me."

Someone compared him to Snow White. "You're literally a Disney princess," another person wrote.

Downey was excited his followers liked the squirrels as much as he did, so he decided to start posting daily videos of Richard and Maxine. In a recent one, he tries to teach Maxine patience as he peels her an avocado.

In another, with a squirrel on his shoulder, he drops wisdom to his furry friend.

"You ain't always going to have the best of days," he tells Maxine. "But when life is down and you're going through a moment, just be still, alright? Don't put too much pressure on yourself."

His followers replied with comments such as, "Thanks so much because that was EXACTLY what I needed to hear right now!!! Grateful."

Shortly after his breakout video in 2022, Downey went to work building a two-story house with a picket fence for the squirrels, and he encouraged his TikTok followers — now numbering more than 1 million — to get involved.

"I created a squirrel wish list so everyone could help me furnish the house and make it cozy," Downey said, noting that it wasn't long before he was swamped with miniature furniture and paintings, a birdbath, holiday decorations and tiny dishes and houseplants.

When Apartment Therapy posted a story about his squirrel-sized home renovations in 2022, packages started to arrive at a faster clip, he said, noting that his followers began to call him the "Squirrel Whisperer."

Fans of Richard and Maxine sent him a tiny working television and a fireplace front. Downey added them to the living room in the wee abode so his little friends could watch the Animal Planet and National Geographic channels in comfort via his streaming service.

"They really do seem to enjoy watching TV," he said. "But more than anything, I'd have to say they like to eat."

Downey leaves out nuts for the squirrels, and he'll occasionally give them grapes and small pieces of avocado. He said he's never been bitten, and his home has never been damaged by the critters, despite some exposed cords on his balcony. Though Newsweek reported earlier this year (2023) that Maxine destroyed a rooftop couch and made off with the insides of a pillow.

"Scrub-jays will show up sometimes and try to steal the nuts," Downey said, referencing the blue jays that live along the Pacific seaboard. "Then it usually gets a little chaotic."

Downey said he never imagined he'd join the ranks of the Texas family that built a squirrel a Whataburger shack, the Mississippi woman who rescued baby squirrels and the woman who opened a chipmunk cafe in Atlanta, Georgia. But he said he's happy to flow with it.

"It's bringing people a lot of joy," he said. "I've heard from people all over the world who enjoy watching the videos."

Now, three years in, his videos attract a community of people who love squirrels, and also are seeking kindness to both animals and humans — just like him.

"This page isn't about the squirrels really, it's about the good vibes," one person wrote on his Instagram.

Last month he heard from the family of a fan of his who died after she spent time in hospice. Downey, who had communicated with her before she died, posted a tearful video saying how lucky he felt to have connected with her. His followers responded in kind with big emotions.

"You brought her so much kindness, happiness and love! Truly to the depths of her soul. She left this plane of existence without fear and with a heart full of squirrels," wrote a follower. "Her transition became even more beautiful because of you, good sir."

Downey said he didn't intend to reach so many people with his squirrel videos, he was just following his instincts. He has always loved animals.

When Downey was growing up in Atlanta, he said he always got a kick out of watching squirrels run up and down trees, but he was more taken by the hermit crab that his first-grade teacher kept in her classroom.

"I'd stay inside at recess to watch it, and at the end of the school year, my teacher gifted the hermit crab to me," he said. "That was my first pet."

He moved to Los Angeles five years ago and works creating social media content, he said.

"I love connecting with people, and now the squirrels have given me a new outlet for that," Downey said, noting that he just finished decorating Richard and Maxine's pad for Halloween.

"Their house is decorated for every holiday — Christmas, Fourth of July, you name it," he said. "They have more decorations than I do."

He records every squirrel milestone — including a gender reveal party he held for laughs in January 2023 for Maxine's new litter of five baby kits — so TikTok viewers can follow the drama unfolding each day on his balcony. The tiny squirrels lived in a palm tree for about three months until they were old enough to leave the nest.

"The gender reveal was mainly for giggles," Downey said, explaining that he didn't know whether her kittens were male or female.

He didn't want to get involved with raising her five young ones.

"I didn't take care of them — I want to keep them wild — but I'm happy if they decide to drop by," Downey said.

"We're not sure who is the father of the babies — people have speculated it's either Richard or Raymond, another squirrel that shows up and takes half the food," he added. "We've nicknamed him Hood Rat Raymond."

Things got more serious in June 2023 when Maxine had another litter, and the kits were in a tree that was trimmed, causing their nest to fall. The workers put the nest in another tree, but Downey thought it wasn't safe. Downey took them in, cared for them, and then returned them to Maxine.

"Rescuing these baby squirrels and reuniting them with mama Maxine, was the greatest feeling ever!" he wrote on his Instagram page.

Someone responded: "Can somebody just donate you a mansion squirrel sanctuary in the woods already. Take Maxine, Richard and all the Grandsquirrels with you."

For now, his balcony residents scamper back and forth between the squirrel house and trees in the neighborhood. He said he sees Richard and Maxine almost every day.

"Maxine will perch on my shoulder, and I'll give her some nuts or avocado and we'll have this perfect little therapeutic moment," Downey said.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Tunisian beekeepers battle extreme heat to keep the buzz alive
levels.body:
Hela Boubaker is a beekeeper in Tunisia, Africa. This year, she has lost 20 beehives because of heat and wildfires.

Hives are carefully placed in the shade. But at 10 a.m. on a late- August Tuesday, it is already 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 degrees Celsius). ""It's not easy," she says. "But at the same time, we are not easy. We won't give up."

Nearly 40 percent of citizens and entire communities rely on farming for their livelihoods. Bees are a big business.

The nation's apiarists must protect their beehives against extreme weather. They are turning to innovative solutions.

Apiarists are beekeepers. Places where they keep beehives are called apiaries.

Extreme Heat And Drought

In recent years, jobs are few and far between. More young Tunisians and many female entrepreneurs are turning to beekeeping. Beekeeping serves as a climate-friendly, sustainable form of self-employment.

Some 13,000 Tunisians work as full-time beekeepers. Thousands more rely on apiary work part-time. Their work produces a combined 280,000 metric tons of honey per year.

For those new to beekeeping in Tunisia, the work has been difficult. Tunisia has faced extreme heat. Temperatures have reached 120 degrees Fahrenheit (49 degrees Celsius). The heat sparked devastating wildfires in 2022 and again in July 2023. This year, the country struggled with a record drought. This is a period of time with less rain than usual. Regions are left without water for weeks at a time.

According to apiarists, the extreme weather has hurt honey production. Bees could produce about 17 pounds (8 kilograms) of honey per hive. In 2023, that's fallen 9 to 11 pounds (4 to 5 kilograms) per hive.

Finding Ways To Keep Bees Alive

Boubaker is an entrepreneur. She is finding ways to keep her bees alive.

She is working with other apiarists. They are adapting to a changing climate. They rent plots of farmers' lands where they place their hives. There, they've added plants that can survive droughts such as lemon trees, thyme and marjoram. This makes sure there is nectar and food sources all year for hives. More delicate flowers and plants wilt in increasingly hot temperatures.

Boubaker moves her hives to different locations, too. In the north, the land is full of pine trees in the mountains. Areas in the south are dry. And the bees also spend time in rich farmlands.

Rotating the hives means they are spread out. Boubaker checks on her 82 colonies every two days. The commute takes six hours and 200 miles (322 kilometers) round trip.

SmartBee App Helps Beekeepers

Innovators are turning to apps to help beekeepers face challenges.

Khaled Bouchoucha is a Tunisian engineer. He has grappled with solving Tunisia's plummeting bee numbers.

"Beekeepers can feel the impact of climate change, but they don't know how to adapt," Bouchoucha said. Climate change is the significant change in the climate of Earth. It happens over a long period of time. Climate change can happen naturally. Today, climate change is largely caused by human activities.

In 2021, Bouchoucha developed and launched SmartBee. This device and app provides beekeepers with real-time data. Keepers can see information about hive temperature, humidity and weight. Humidity is the amount of water vapor in the air.

Tunisia has seen record-setting scorching temperatures of 120 degrees Fahrenheit (49 degrees Celsius). The heat sparked devastating wildfires in 2022 and again in July 2023. According to researchers and apiarists, the extreme weather has nearly halved honey production. Bees could produce an average of 17 pounds (8 kilograms) of honey per hive. In 2023, it's fallen to 9 to 11 pounds (4 to 5 kilograms) per hive.

More delicate flowers and plants wilt in increasingly hot temperatures.
